title: Finite Nonsignalling Resources Suffice To Simulate Entangled Qubits
authors: Ziao Tang, Xin Wang, Ge Bai
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32319v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations of partially entangled qubits. Here we resolve this problem by showing that every fixed pure two-qubit state admits an exact simulation of all local projective-measurement statistics using shared randomness and finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich (PR) boxes, without communication or postselection. The boxes operate in parallel, with a worst-case bound independent of the measurement settings: at most [MATH] calls for the Schmidt state [MATH], [MATH]. The key is an exact finite-selection method that reduces input-dependent continuous sampling to a choice from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented through a finite PR-box network. The construction extends to arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs. This reveals a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of the resources needed to simulate them, shedding light on the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.
tldr: The paper shows that finitely many Popescu-Rohrlich boxes plus shared randomness can exactly simulate all local projective-measurement statistics of any fixed pure two-qubit entangled state, and extends the construction to mixed states and binary-outcome POVMs.
motivation: A longstanding question in Bell nonlocality is whether finite-alphabet nonsignalling resources can reproduce the continuum of measurement correlations exhibited by partially entangled qubits.
method: The authors introduce an exact finite-selection method that converts input-dependent continuous sampling into choosing from a fixed-length shared random list, implemented via a finite parallel PR-box network without communication or postselection.
result: They obtain worst-case bounds independent of measurement settings: at most finitely many PR-box calls for the Schmidt state, with the construction covering arbitrary mixed two-qubit states and local binary-outcome POVMs.
conclusion: The work establishes a fundamental separation between the continuity of quantum measurement correlations and the alphabet size of nonsignalling resources needed to simulate them, clarifying the resource-theoretic structure of Bell nonlocality.

title: Quantum Secret Sharing From Css qLDPC Codes: Computable Access Structures, Accessible Logical Dimension, And Topology-Aware Network Cost
authors: Saif Al-Kuwari Malik Mouaji
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32428v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum secret sharing (QSS) schemes can be constructed from quantum error-correcting codes, but characterizing their access structures and implementation costs becomes challenging for finite-length, high-rate quantum low-density parity-check (qLDPC) codes. We develop an exact computational framework for QSS induced by CSS qLDPC codes. The framework characterizes authorized, forbidden, and intermediate coalitions using restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra, and introduces the accessible logical dimension \(\kappa(A)\), defined through the symplectic rank of locally supported logical classes, to refine the characterization of intermediate coalitions. We further incorporate physical network constraints through separate Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth costs, and treat the partitioning of physical qubits into participants as an explicit design variable. Numerical experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes verify the predicted complement duality and monotonicity properties and show substantial variation in access transitions and network costs. For the codes studied, the bivariate bicycle instance exhibits the sharpest transition, while network embedding costs vary by more than an order of magnitude across physical topologies. We also show that participant partitioning can substantially improve block-level security and reconstruction thresholds. These results provide a practical bridge between the algebraic structure of CSS qLDPC codes, the graded accessibility of quantum secrets, and the physical constraints of networked QSS implementations.
tldr: The paper develops an exact computational framework for quantum secret sharing based on finite-length CSS qLDPC codes, characterizing access structures and topology-aware network implementation costs.
motivation: Quantum secret sharing from quantum error-correcting codes is promising, but finite-length high-rate qLDPC codes make access structures and physical network costs difficult to characterize.
method: The authors use restricted parity-check matrices and binary linear algebra to classify coalitions, introduce an accessible logical dimension via symplectic rank, and model network costs through Tanner-incidence, Steiner-routing, and scheduling-depth terms.
result: Numerical experiments on four CSS qLDPC codes verify complement duality and monotonicity, reveal substantial variation in access transitions and network costs, and show that participant partitioning can improve security and reconstruction thresholds.
conclusion: The framework bridges algebraic structure, graded secret accessibility, and physical network constraints for practical networked quantum secret sharing implementations.

deep_read.methodology_analysis: The methodology centers on an exact algebraic characterization of QSS access structures for CSS qLDPC codes. For a given coalition of participants, the authors restrict the code's parity-check matrices to the qubits held by that coalition and use binary linear algebra to determine whether the coalition can access logical information. Authorized coalitions correspond to those that can reconstruct the secret, forbidden coalitions cannot access any logical information, and intermediate coalitions have partial access. To quantify partial access, they introduce the accessible logical dimension κ(A), computed as the symplectic rank of the space of logical operators that can be implemented locally on the coalition's qubits. This provides a graded measure of accessibility. The framework also models the physical implementation by mapping code qubits to participants and then to network nodes, with costs for Tanner-incidence (connections between check and data qubits), Steiner-routing (network paths), and scheduling depth (time steps). title: Measurement Speed Limit And Cram\'er-Rao Bound For Time-averaged Estimators
authors: Andreas Dechant Hiroyuki Odajima
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We consider a measured system [MATH] containing a parameter [MATH] of interest and the problem of estimating this parameter by observing a second, coupled measurement system [MATH]. We show that, in thermodynamic equilibrium, the Fisher information of [MATH] associated with the parameter is bounded by that of [MATH], implying that conservative interactions between [MATH] and [MATH] reduce the precision of parameter estimation. Conversely, out of equilibrium, we show that the Fisher information of [MATH] can exceed that of [MATH], so that non-conservative interactions can potentially increase the precision of parameter estimation. For idealized, back-action-free measurements, where the coupling to [MATH] does not perturb [MATH], we derive a speed limit for the increase of Fisher information of [MATH]. This speed limit only depends on the properties of the measured system [MATH] and places a fundamental bound on the precision of any back-action-free measurement. As a corollary, we obtain a generalized Cram\'er-Rao bound (CRB) for time-averaged estimators. We illustrate our results for linear dynamics and suggest a scheme for disturbance-free non-equilibrium sensing with improved accuracy.
tldr: The paper derives fundamental bounds on parameter-estimation precision and measurement speed using Fisher information for a measured system coupled to a probe, contrasting equilibrium and non-equilibrium regimes.
motivation: Parameter estimation is limited by the physical interaction between the system of interest and the measurement device, but general thermodynamic and dynamical constraints on achievable precision and measurement speed remain important to clarify.
method: The authors analyze Fisher information of a parameter in a measured system and a coupled measurement system, proving bounds in thermodynamic equilibrium and non-equilibrium, and deriving a speed limit for Fisher-information growth in back-action-free measurements.
result: In equilibrium, conservative interactions cannot increase Fisher information beyond that of the measured system, whereas out of equilibrium non-conservative interactions can enhance precision; a generalized Cramér-Rao bound for time-averaged estimators follows from the speed limit.
conclusion: The work establishes fundamental limits on measurement precision and speed, and suggests disturbance-free non-equilibrium sensing schemes with improved accuracy.

title: Mutual Information Across Quantum Reference Frame Perspectives
authors: Leonardo Valente, Carla Ferradini, Flaminia Giacomini, Viktoria Kabel
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31729v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In quantum information theory, standard notions typically presuppose a fixed partition of the world into subsystems, encoded in a tensor product structure of the Hilbert space. Yet, in some scenarios, the subsystem structure is not uniquely fixed. A case in point is the description of subsystems relative to different quantum reference frames (QRFs), where the tensor product structure, although fixed in a specific QRF, changes across different QRFs. Such a relativity of subsystems underlies many interesting features of QRFs, such as the relativity of entanglement, entropy, and coherence. It also raises a broader question: how do we compare the information across different subsystem perspectives, especially when the corresponding subsystem algebras overlap? Here, we propose a notion of quantum mutual information across different QRF perspectives, which captures the correlations between subsystems relative to different frames of reference. To do so, we focus on an algebraic definition of subsystems. Studying in detail the union and overlap between subsystem algebras relative to different QRFs, we find that the usual definition of mutual information in terms of the chain law overcounts the information associated to the overlap. Based on this insight, we propose a modified chain law and show that the resulting notion of mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures found in the literature [1]. Our investigations not only provide a way to quantify the relation between different QRF perspectives from an information-theoretic point of view but also sheds light on some important features of quantum information in absence of a fixed tensor product structure.
tldr: The paper proposes a frame-dependent notion of quantum mutual information for comparing correlations between subsystems described relative to different quantum reference frames, where the tensor product structure is not fixed.
motivation: Standard quantum information measures assume a fixed subsystem decomposition, but quantum reference frames can change the subsystem structure and make entropy, coherence, and entanglement frame-dependent. A principled way is needed to compare information across such perspectives, especially when subsystem algebras overlap.
method: The authors use an algebraic definition of subsystems and analyze unions and overlaps of subsystem algebras associated with different quantum reference frames. They identify an overcounting in the usual chain-law definition of mutual information and propose a modified chain law.
result: The modified mutual information satisfies subadditivity and connects naturally to other measures in the literature, while correctly accounting for information associated with overlapping subsystem algebras.
conclusion: The work provides an information-theoretic framework for quantifying correlations across quantum reference frame perspectives and clarifies features of quantum information when no fixed tensor product structure is available.

deep_read.detailed_summary: The paper addresses the problem of defining quantum mutual information between subsystems that are described relative to different quantum reference frames (QRFs). In standard quantum information, a fixed tensor product structure of the Hilbert space is assumed, but when comparing descriptions from different QRFs, the subsystem decomposition changes, and the corresponding subsystem algebras may overlap. The authors adopt an algebraic approach, representing subsystems by von Neumann algebras, and analyze the union and intersection of algebras associated with different QRFs. They show that the usual chain rule for mutual information, I(A:B) = S(A) + S(B) - S(AB), overcounts correlations because it double-counts the information in the overlap of the algebras. To correct this, they propose a modified chain law that subtracts the entropy of the overlap, leading to a new definition of mutual information across QRFs. They prove that this quantity satisfies subadditivity and demonstrate that it reduces to known measures in special cases, such as when the algebras are independent or when one is contained in the other. The work provides an information-theoretic tool to quantify correlations between different QRF perspectives and highlights subtleties of quantum information without a fixed tensor product structure.

Proposes a modified chain law that subtracts the entropy of the overlap, yielding a new definition of mutual information across QRFs.

Provides an algebraic framework for comparing information across different subsystem perspectives, advancing the understanding of quantum information without a fixed tensor product structure.

They consider two QRFs, each inducing a different decomposition of the total algebra into subsystem algebras, and study the union and intersection of these algebras. The usual mutual information is defined via the chain law using von Neumann entropy. The key methodological step is to analyze the overlap algebra and show that the standard chain law double-counts entropy contributions from the overlap. They then modify the chain law by subtracting the entropy of the overlap, leading to a new definition. The proof of subadditivity likely relies on properties of von Neumann entropy and the structure of the algebras, such as monotonicity under completely positive maps. The approach is general and does not rely on specific QRF transformations, making it applicable to a wide range of scenarios.

Actually, the paper states that the usual chain law overcounts by the entropy of the overlap, so the modified version subtracts S(A∩B). More precisely, they propose I(A:B) = S(A) + S(B) - S(A∪B) - S(A∩B) or similar. The paper proves subadditivity: I(A:B) ≥ 0, and possibly stronger properties. They show that when A and B are independent (A∩B trivial), the formula reduces to the standard mutual information. When one algebra is contained in the other, it reduces to a conditional entropy-like quantity. The results are theoretical, with no numerical values, but the proofs establish the consistency of the measure.

Proves subadditivity, ensuring the measure is physically meaningful.

title: Traceable Quantum Secret Sharing
authors: Mengyan Qiao, Jian Long, Yu Li, Zhu Cao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32218v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum secret sharing protects distributed quantum information against unauthorized reconstruction, yet existing schemes provide no intrinsic accountability when shares are leaked or forged. This missing capability is particularly relevant in realistic distributed settings, where compromised participants may either expose valid shares or maliciously interfere with reconstruction. Here we establish a framework for traceable quantum secret sharing under these two threat models. We introduce leakage-verifiable and traceable quantum secret sharing (LVT-QSS), which attributes leaked shares through an explicit leakage verification mechanism, and malicious-traceable and accountable quantum secret sharing (MTA-QSS), which identifies participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. We formulate security definitions for both settings and prove that the proposed protocols satisfy the corresponding guarantees against the relevant adversaries. Numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise further quantify the robustness of the proposed schemes and identify verification as the dominant noise sensitive stage. These results incorporate accountability into quantum secret sharing and provide a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.
tldr: The paper introduces traceable quantum secret sharing protocols that add accountability against leaked or forged shares in distributed quantum communication.
motivation: Existing quantum secret sharing schemes protect distributed quantum information but lack intrinsic accountability when participants leak valid shares or submit forged shares during reconstruction.
method: The authors formulate leakage-verifiable and traceable QSS (LVT-QSS) and malicious-traceable and accountable QSS (MTA-QSS), define security against the corresponding adversaries, and prove protocol guarantees.
result: Security definitions and proofs are provided for both threat models, and numerical simulations under per-share depolarizing noise quantify robustness, identifying verification as the dominant noise-sensitive stage.
conclusion: The work incorporates accountability into quantum secret sharing and provides a foundation for traceable distributed quantum cryptography.

deep_read.detailed_summary: This paper introduces two frameworks for adding accountability to quantum secret sharing (QSS): leakage-verifiable and traceable QSS (LVT-QSS) and malicious-traceable and accountable QSS (MTA-QSS). The motivation is that standard QSS schemes protect against unauthorized reconstruction but offer no mechanism to attribute leaked shares or identify participants who submit forged shares during reconstruction. LVT-QSS addresses the threat of a participant leaking a valid share: it provides an explicit leakage verification mechanism that can determine whether a given share was leaked by a specific participant. title: Fundamental Bound On Wigner Negativity Generation From Environmental Collisions
authors: Isaac Layton, Takahiro Sagawa, Ken Funo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32315v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Beyond quadratic potentials, classical evolution laws are typically thought to arise from quantum theory as an approximate description. Here we show that classical evolution laws can emerge exactly, provided the environment interacts with the system via collisions. We use this to derive an inequality that lower bounds the distribution of environmental momentum kicks by the absolute value of the Fourier transform of the potential. We show that violating this inequality is necessary and sufficient for a non-quadratic potential to generate negativity from the set of positive Wigner functions. A simple consequence of this is a lower bound on the heating rate for a quantum system to evolve effectively classically. We illustrate our results using the theory of a levitated nanoparticle subject to photon recoil and background gas collisions. We derive the strength of external potential needed to generate Wigner negative states in an optical tweezer and propose an experimental test of whether a nanoparticle in an optical lattice is operating in a non-classical regime.

motivation: Classical evolution is usually viewed as an approximation to quantum theory, but the authors ask when classical laws can emerge exactly and what thermodynamic/nonclassicality constraints accompany this emergence.
method: They model the environment as colliding with the system, derive an inequality lower-bounding the distribution of environmental momentum kicks, and connect violation of this bound to the generation of Wigner negativity; they illustrate the result with a levitated nanoparticle under photon recoil and gas collisions.
result: The inequality provides a necessary and sufficient condition for non-quadratic potentials to create negativity from positive Wigner functions, and yields a lower bound on the heating rate required for effectively classical evolution.
conclusion: The work establishes a fundamental link between environmental collisions, Wigner negativity generation, and heating, and proposes experimental tests with optically trapped nanoparticles.

title: Entangled Logical Qubits On A Superconducting Quantum Processor
authors: Robin Harper, Xanda C. Kolesnikow, Campbell K. Mclauchlan, Georgia M. Nixon, Stephen D. Bartlett, Benjamin J. Brown
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32347v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We demonstrate high-fidelity logical qubit operations using , a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits that are capable of fast reset. Using strategies to exclude underperforming components together with noise informed decoding, we routinely produce surface codes at distance-3 and distance-5 with logical error per round below 1\%. We demonstrate entanglement between two logical qubits, where logical Bell-state fidelities above 93\% are observed for entanglement created via lattice surgery. With three logical qubits and lattice surgery, we perform logical teleportation of a range of states and gates, observing fidelities in the range 78\% - 93\%. Using reset to reduce qubit leakage, we show that repeated rounds of stabilizer measurements continue to exhibit improvements in a stability experiment up to [MATH] over 170 measurement rounds.
tldr: An experimental demonstration on a 120-qubit superconducting processor of distance-3 and distance-5 surface codes with sub-1% logical error per round, including logical Bell states, lattice-surgery teleportation, and a long-duration stability experiment.
motivation: Fault-tolerant quantum computation requires logical qubits whose error rates are suppressed below their constituent physical qubits; demonstrating high-fidelity logical operations and entangled logical qubits on real hardware is a key milestone toward that goal.
method: Using a square-lattice array of 120 coupled superconducting qubits with fast reset, the authors exclude underperforming components, apply noise-informed decoding, and implement surface codes at distance 3 and 5 together with lattice-surgery-based entangling and teleportation operations, plus a stability experiment over 170 rounds.
result: Logical error per round below 1% at both distances, logical Bell-state fidelities above 93% for lattice-surgery entanglement, logical teleportation fidelities of 78%-93% across three logical qubits, and continued error suppression with increasing code distance in the stability experiment.
conclusion: The results show that superconducting hardware can support high-fidelity logical qubit operations and entanglement, providing strong evidence that scaling surface-code architectures is a viable path toward fault tolerance.

title: Optimal Control Of A Fluxonium Circuit With The Q-pronto Numerical Method
authors: John Barta, Brian D. Isakov, Pablo Aramburu Sanchez, Jieqiu Shao, Tam\'as Kalm\'ar, Trevyn F. Q. Larson, Marco M. Nicotra, Andr\'as Gyenis
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31885v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Optimizing the control of large quantum systems is a resource-intensive task, where the convergence rate of the underlying iterative schemes is crucial. The recently developed Quantum Projection Operator-Based Newton Method for Trajectory Optimization (Q-PRONTO) offers a unique quadratic convergence for controlling quantum states, while most model-based solvers guarantee only an approximately linear convergence rate. As a proof of concept, here, we design and benchmark single-qubit gates optimized by Q-PRONTO based on the circuit Hamiltonian of a fluxonium superconducting qubit. To ensure that we can apply a long string of arbitrary pulses to the circuit, we modify the firmware associated with the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) by altering its memory allocation. We characterize the performance of the optimal solutions using standard randomized benchmarking and achieve a total error per gate of [MATH].
tldr: The paper applies the Q-PRONTO optimal-control method to design and benchmark single-qubit gates for a fluxonium superconducting circuit, including firmware modifications to enable long pulse sequences.
motivation: Optimal control of large quantum systems is resource-intensive, and most model-based solvers converge only approximately linearly; Q-PRONTO promises quadratic convergence, motivating a practical test on a real superconducting-qubit Hamiltonian.
method: The authors use Q-PRONTO to optimize control pulses based on a fluxonium circuit Hamiltonian, modify QICK firmware memory allocation to support long arbitrary pulse strings, and characterize gate performance with randomized benchmarking.
result: They implement optimized single-qubit gates on a fluxonium device and report a total error per gate measured by randomized benchmarking, demonstrating the feasibility of Q-PRONTO-based control in this platform.
conclusion: The work provides a proof-of-concept that Q-PRONTO can be used for high-fidelity control of fluxonium qubits and highlights firmware-level considerations for applying long optimized pulse sequences experimentally.

title: Two-Layer Verification For Fault-Tolerant Magic-State Preparation In High-Rate Quantum Codes
authors: Hayato Goto Naoyuki Kanomata
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32267v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Encoded magic states are essential for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but their resource-efficient preparation in high-rate quantum codes remains challenging. To address this limitation, we propose two-layer verification, which combines local verification of independently prepared subblocks with logical verification after their embedding into a target code. This hierarchy detects harmful error patterns, including even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that are invisible to a collective product check alone. We demonstrate this scheme for a [MATH] code by constructing a circuit that embeds three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into the target code. Circuit-level simulations of [MATH]- and [MATH]-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance. These results demonstrate the potential of two-layer verification as a design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.
tldr: The paper proposes a two-layer verification scheme for fault-tolerant magic-state preparation in high-rate quantum codes, combining local subblock verification with logical verification after embedding.
motivation: Encoded magic states are necessary for universal fault-tolerant quantum computation, but preparing them resource-efficiently in high-rate codes is difficult because some harmful logical error patterns evade simple collective checks.
method: The authors introduce two-layer verification: independently prepared subblocks are locally verified, then embedded into a target code and logically verified. They construct a circuit embedding three verified seven-qubit Steane-code magic states into a high-rate code and perform circuit-level simulations.
result: Circuit-level simulations of magic-state preparation show logical-error suppression consistent with the code distance, detecting even-parity logical-eigenvalue flips that a collective product check alone would miss.
conclusion: Two-layer verification is presented as a promising design principle for reliable magic-state preparation in quantum codes encoding multiple logical qubits.

title: Robustness Of Quantum Correlations And Controlled Teleportation Fidelity Under Noisy Channels
authors: S. Archana, Aditi Das, Venkat Abhignan, R. Muthuganesan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32049v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In distributed quantum computing, quantum networks provide a potential infrastructure for long-range quantum information processing. Controlled quantum teleportation (CQT) is a key practically relevant protocol that can connect two parties on a network and enables a third party, the controller to allow or abort the secure teleportation of an arbitrary single-qubit state between the two parties. We investigate the robustness of a three-qubit GHZ resource under bit-flip, phase-flip, depolarizing, and amplitude-damping noise. Using the Kraus-operator formalism, we characterize the noisy resource through multipartite quantum discord, genuine multipartite concurrence (GMC), localizable entanglement (LE), and CQT fidelity. We also outline a proof-of-concept photonic implementation for preparing the three-qubit GHZ resource and realizing the CQT protocol, which could enable experimental investigation of the effects of noise. Our results show that bit-flip and amplitude-damping noise generally preserve useful mutipartite quantum correlations over broader noise parameter ranges. Interestingly, multipartite discord exhibits freezing under bit-flip noise over a finite parameter regime. Moreover, discord can persist beyond the sudden death of genuine multipartite entanglement, revealing the distinct robustness of nonclassical correlations. We further demonstrate that CQT fidelity which characterizes the performance of CQT can exceed the classical threshold even after GMC vanishes, while LE more closely reflects the operational usefulness of the noisy resource. These findings highlight the complementary roles of quantum correlations and entanglement in assessing the resilience of GHZ-based protocols.

title: Fidelity Dynamics Of A Jaynes--Cummings Qubit Under Markovian And Non-Markovian Coupling Noise
authors: Fang Wang, Da-Wei Luo, Ting Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31938v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We analytically investigate the fidelity dynamics of a Jaynes--Cummings qubit coupled to a single-mode cavity in the presence of stochastic fluctuations of the qubit--cavity coupling. Such fluctuations naturally arise in cavity- and circuit-QED platforms due to fabrication imperfections, control-field noise, mechanical vibrations, and environmental disturbances. Since the qubit--cavity coupling governs the rate of coherent energy and information exchange, understanding the effects of its fluctuations is essential for assessing the performance of quantum communication, quantum sensing, and quantum information-processing protocols. We consider both Gaussian white noise and Ornstein--Uhlenbeck noise with finite correlation time as models for the coupling fluctuations. Exploiting the closed dynamics within each excitation manifold, we derive exact analytical expressions for the noise-averaged density matrix and the fidelity relative to the ideal noiseless evolution. We show that the fidelity is determined by a single decoherence factor governed by the integrated noise correlation function, establishing a direct connection between microscopic coupling fluctuations and macroscopic coherence loss. In the white-noise limit, the fidelity decays exponentially, whereas finite noise correlation times produce nonexponential decay and slower coherence loss. We further show that the crossover between Markovian-like and non-Markovian regimes is controlled by the ratio of the noise correlation rate to the coherent coupling strength, and that decoherence increases with photon number because of the enhanced effective qubit--cavity coupling. These results provide a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence induced by stochastic coupling fluctuations and for evaluating the robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.

conclusion: The work provides a unified analytical framework for quantifying decoherence from stochastic coupling fluctuations and for assessing robustness of cavity-QED protocols under correlated noise.

title: Quantum Complexity And Stabilizer-State Expansions: From Pairing To Deformation In Fermionic Systems
authors: Caroline E. P. Robin S. Momme Hengstenberg
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31792v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Understanding how collective phenomena such as pairing and deformation emerge in interacting fermionic systems, and how the correlations underlying them shape the resources required for their simulation, is a central challenge in many-body physics. We investigate various aspects of quantum complexity in a fermionic system exhibiting two main forms of collectivity, specifically deformation and pairing, through entanglement, non-stabilizerness, and fermionic non-Gaussianity. In the deformed phase, high entanglement coexists with low non-stabilizerness, while the superfluid pairing phase, by contrast, exhibits substantial multipartite entanglement and non-stabilizerness, together with maximal fermionic anti-flatness. In a second step we examine how to describe the phase diagram of the system in a classically scalable and symmetry-preserving way, by combining stabilizer-state expansion and variational basis optimization. A physics-guided decomposition of the Hamiltonian identifies the relevant stabilizer states, which can be constructed from graph states. A single stabilizer state captures the deformed phase to a large extent, and, although the number of stabilizer states required to describe the pairing phase grows exponentially with system size, a symmetry-preserving basis rotation yields a high-fidelity approximation using far fewer states. This rotated state can then serve as a practical starting point for quantum refinement.

title: Temporal Degeneracy Limits Message Passing Decoding Of Qldpc Codes Under Repeated Noisy Syndrome Measurements
authors: Dimitris Chytas, Nithin Raveendran, Bane Vasi\'{c}
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31877v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Practical quantum computations can require logical error rates of [MATH] or lower. Quantum low-density parity-check (QLDPC) codes are promising candidates for reaching such rates with low qubit overhead, provided that their syndromes can be decoded efficiently. Repeated noisy syndrome measurements introduce temporal degeneracy into the space-time decoding graph. We characterize the temporal kernel, whose vectors have zero total data parity, and show that it is generated by elementary temporal codewords of weight [MATH], where [MATH] is the variable-node degree. For [MATH]-regular parity-check matrices with fixed degrees [MATH] and girth greater than four, we derive counting bounds and construct degenerate error patterns of weight [MATH] for even [MATH] and [MATH] for odd [MATH], with multiplicity [MATH] in the blocklength [MATH] and number of measurement rounds [MATH]. Under the isolation assumption, these patterns cause local failures of deterministic isotropic message-passing decoders under a flooding schedule. These failures depend on the node degrees rather than the minimum distance; for the bivariate bicycle (BB) codes considered, their weight is equal to four. Monte carlo simulations and fixed-weight importance sampling quantify harmful low-weight degenerate error patterns for the min-sum (MS) decoder beyond the isolation assumption. Motivated by the identified symmetries, we propose space-time anisotropic min-sum decoding with syndrome-guided realizations. Its complexity is linear in the number of Tanner graph edges for fixed maximum number of iterations and number of decoders. Numerical results on BB codes show threshold-like behavior acrossthe tested code sizes and improved failure probabilities relative to MS decoding with ordered statistics decoding post-processing.

conclusion: Temporal degeneracy imposes fundamental limits on isotropic message-passing decoding of QLDPC codes, and symmetry-informed anisotropic decoding can improve performance while retaining linear complexity.

title: Graphical Rigidity Of Continuous Variable Graph States Under Gaussian Local Transformations
authors: Fr\'ed\'eric Grosshans Giorgio Ciliberto
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31933v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multimode entangled pure Gaussian states are an essential resource for continuous variable (CV) quantum information processing. Menicucci et al. [2011] have shown how to describe them as graphs with complex adjacency matrices. Among such complex graph states (CGSs), quantum optics experimental setups straightforwardly display correlations described by purely imaginary graph states (iRGSs) whereas theoretical literature favors off-diagonal real graph state (RGS) descriptions, which actually reflect the entanglement structure in the infinite squeezing limit [Gonzalez-Arciniegas et al. 2021]. We study them beyond this ideal case, thus establishing in the finite squeezing regime an equivalence criterion for the generic case of CGSs through a graph propagating set of conditions which either finds a Gaussian Local Unitary (GLU) converting one state to another or gives a proof of impossibility if such a GLU does not exist. In the experimentally relevant case of the conversion between iRGSs and RGSs, the set of conditions results in simple relations between the topologies of the equivalent real and imaginary graphs. Finally, we show that the canonical forms of iRGSs and RGSs imply that the topology of the CV real and imaginary graph states are too rigid to admit any exact qumode local-addition analogue to the qubit complementation or qudit local-addition, thus demonstrating the non-existence of any exact qumode local-addition for these states. We however define an approximate one when the squeezing is strong enough.
tldr: The paper establishes equivalence criteria for continuous-variable complex graph states under Gaussian local unitaries and shows rigidity of real and imaginary graph-state topologies in the finite-squeezing regime.
motivation: Multimode entangled Gaussian states are key resources for CV quantum information, but the relation between experimentally natural imaginary graph states and theoretically favored real graph states is not fully understood beyond infinite squeezing.
method: The authors derive a graph-propagating set of conditions that either constructs a Gaussian local unitary mapping between complex graph states or proves impossibility, specializing to conversions between imaginary and real graph states.
result: They obtain simple topological relations for equivalent real and imaginary graphs and prove that CV graph-state topologies are too rigid to admit an exact qumode local-addition analogue of qubit complementation, though an approximate version exists at strong squeezing.
conclusion: The work clarifies Gaussian local equivalence of CV graph states and highlights structural rigidity, with approximate local-addition operations only in the strong-squeezing limit.

The central problem is to determine when two such states are equivalent under Gaussian local unitaries (GLUs) in the finite squeezing regime, beyond the ideal infinite-squeezing case.

title: Noise-Assisted Quantum Entanglement: Memory-Enhanced Coherence In Stochastic Jaynes-Cummings Dynamics
authors: Fang Wang, Quanzhen Ding, Jun Jing, Ting Yu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31947v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We investigate qubit entanglement dynamics in a two-qubit cavity system with stochastically fluctuating coupling strength, comparing white noise (Markovian) and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise (non-Markovian) processes. We analytically solve the system dynamics for both Fock and coherent cavity states and systematically characterize how initial qubit configurations affect entanglement generation and preservation. Our results reveal distinct dynamical regimes: in the Fock-state cavity, initial states in the single-excitation subspace generate robust qubit entanglement in decoherence-free subspaces, while initially entangled states in the double-excitation subspace exhibit inevitable decay without protective symmetries. For coherent cavities, we identify a critical photon-number threshold in the intermediate coherent-state amplitude regime where dynamics transition from low-frequency to high-frequency entanglement oscillations, while universal entanglement loss occurs at large amplitudes. Remarkable resilience against entanglement sudden death emerges under strong non-Markovian noise with long correlation times, where repeated revivals occur. These findings establish cavity photon statistics and environmental memory time as key control parameters for engineering qubit entanglement dynamics in qubit-cavity systems, revealing how system-environment correlations govern quantum information preservation.

method: The authors analytically solve the stochastic Jaynes-Cummings dynamics for Fock and coherent cavity states with white and Ornstein-Uhlenbeck noise, comparing different initial qubit configurations.
result: Fock-state single-excitation subspaces support robust entanglement via decoherence-free subspaces, coherent cavities exhibit a photon-number threshold, and strong non-Markovian noise with long correlation times produces entanglement revivals and resilience to sudden death.
conclusion: Cavity photon statistics and environmental memory time are key control parameters for engineering qubit entanglement in cavity-QED systems.

title: The Entire Quantum Computer On A Classical Leash
authors: Yael Tauman Kalai, Dakshita Khurana, Justin Raizes
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31775v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: We show that a classical client with no quantum hardware can use a single untrusted and potentially malicious quantum server as if it were its own trusted quantum computer. Through the server, the client can privately choose and run quantum computations, prepare quantum states, and process quantum states supplied by other parties. It can also keep quantum memory on the server, hidden from the server itself, and use that memory in later computations so its quantum state persists across rounds of interaction. Together, these capabilities let a purely classical party act as a quantum party in a variety of interactive protocols. We expect this virtual quantum computer to be a broadly useful tool. As immediate applications, we resolve two known open problems: (1) classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and (2) remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states. Underlying all of these results is a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, which we construct assuming only the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors.
tldr: A purely classical client can securely outsource quantum computation, quantum state preparation, and persistent quantum memory to a single untrusted quantum server, effectively obtaining a virtual quantum computer.
motivation: Classical users lack quantum hardware, so protocols are needed that let them delegate quantum computations and state preparation to an untrusted server while preserving privacy and correctness even against a malicious server.
method: The authors construct a general-purpose, maliciously secure two-party computation protocol between a classical client and a quantum server, relying only on the post-quantum hardness of learning with errors, and then build delegation, remote state preparation, and persistent quantum memory on top of it.
result: The framework yields a virtual quantum computer for classical parties, resolving two open problems: classical verification of quantum sampling with negligible computational soundness error, and remote state preparation of arbitrary efficiently preparable quantum states.
conclusion: The work provides a broadly applicable cryptographic toolkit enabling classical parties to act as quantum parties in interactive protocols, though its contributions are cryptographic/complexity-theoretic rather than focused on entanglement, entropy, or nonlocality.

title: Quantum Theory Of Laser Noise In Coherent-scattering Levitated Optomechanics
authors: Davide Candoli, Andreu Riera-Campeny, Lorenzo Dania, Oscar Schmitt Kremer, Johannes Piotrowski, Jayadev Vijayan, Lukas Novotny, Martin Frimmer, Oriol Romero-Isart, Carlos Gonzalez-Ballestero
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32368v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: State purity is a key resource for experimental tests of quantum mechanics with massive objects. Cavity cooling of a levitated nanoparticle via coherent scattering stands out as a strategy to prepare highly pure states of its roto-translational motion. In several cases, though, the performance of cooling by coherent scattering is limited by the classical fluctuations of the laser field. Here we present a quantum theory of coherent-scattering experiments which includes the effect of the laser amplitude and phase noise. We derive a master equation for the noise-averaged particle's dynamics, valid for both center-of-mass and rotational degrees of freedom, and quantify the cooling performance for different levels of noise in state-of-the-art experiments. We compute approximate analytical expressions for the laser-noise-induced heating rates and excess phonon number in both regimes of weak and strong optomechanical coupling. Moreover, our model can be applied to laser noise processes with generic power spectral densities and finite correlation times. This work offers a toolbox to quantify and optimize the state purity in coherent-scattering experiments, and opens new avenues towards the preparation of quantum states with levitated systems.

method: The authors derive a master equation for the noise-averaged center-of-mass and rotational dynamics of the levitated particle and compute analytical heating rates and excess phonon occupations for weak and strong optomechanical coupling.
result: The theory predicts how laser amplitude and phase noise degrade cooling and set excess phonon numbers, with expressions applicable to generic noise spectral densities and finite correlation times.
conclusion: The work provides a toolbox for optimizing state purity in coherent-scattering levitated optomechanics and supports future quantum-state preparation with levitated systems.

title: Verified Pauli-Product Measurement Compilation For Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computation
authors: Jens Palsberg John Zhuoyang Ye
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31694v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-tolerant quantum compilers implement gates through Pauli-product measurements and classical feedback. Verifying such a compiler requires reasoning about the quantum state and the recorded outcomes together: a correction reads an outcome, a gate's internal outcomes must be hidden from its caller, and an application's outcomes must survive optimization. We introduce QPPM, a language for Pauli-product measurement programs, with a weakest-precondition semantics over store-indexed matrix assertions, following quantum Hoare logic with classical variables. Every program terminates, so the Hoare logic is a syntactic presentation of weakest preconditions whose soundness and relative completeness are immediate. Its value is that component specifications compose. All results are mechanized in Lean. We verify lowering of Clifford+[MATH] circuits to QPPM with private outcomes and supplied magic states, and an optimizer that eliminates measurements, fuses and reorders rotations, and schedules logical rounds while preserving every outcome that subsequent code can read. A compositional approximation relation bounds the effect of synthesis error on specifications and on output trace distance, and a certificate-checked pipeline selects, among synthesized circuits that meet the user's error limit, the one with the lowest certified depth bound. On QASMBench, verified fusion and scheduling reduce logical measurement depth by a median of 17.9\%, and complete source-to-QPPM allowances are certified for all 35 valid selected small-suite inputs.

conclusion: Compositional, machine-checked specifications for Pauli-product measurement programs provide a practical verification path for fault-tolerant compiler pipelines and their optimizations, with quantified synthesis-error bounds on output trace distance.

title: Trident: Efficient Load Verification For Yoked Surface Codes Using A Three-Level Memory Hierarchy
authors: Gunagya Singh Mamak, Suhas Vittal, Kabir Dubey, Kaitlin N. Smith, Moinuddin K. Qureshi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32152v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fault-Tolerant Quantum Computers (FTQCs) commonly use the surface code to encode program qubits as error-corrected logical qubits. Unfortunately, the surface code has a poor encoding rate, so recent work has proposed Yoked Surface Codes (YSCs), which concatenate the surface code with a high-rate quantum code. The surface code qubits in YSCs are protected by the checks, or yokes, of the high-rate code. YSCs have 1D and 2D variants, which are [MATH] and [MATH] more efficient than the surface code, respectively. Modern FTQC architectures use a two-level hierarchy: surface codes perform logical operations (compute) while 2D YSCs store idle program qubits (memory). To load a qubit from memory, the FTQC first performs retrieval, which logically moves a program qubit from a 2D YSC into a surface code (8 cycles). However, retrieval is not fault-tolerant, so the FTQC must verify the load by measuring all the yokes of the 2D YSC (178 cycles). As verification dominates memory access latency, eliminating it can provide a speedup of [MATH]. Our goal is to reduce the verification overhead of 2D YSCs while retaining their storage efficiency. We exploit the fact that 1D YSCs, though less storage-efficient, incur negligible verification latency. We propose Trident, which expands the two-level hierarchy into a three-level hierarchy by adding a small intermediate level containing a 1D YSC (L1). If most loads hit L1 rather than L2 (2D YSC tier), it can significantly reduce verification overhead. We present two variants: Trident-D (demand-driven) and Trident-P (prefetch-driven), which achieve speedups of [MATH] and [MATH], respectively, while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.
tldr: Trident introduces a three-level memory hierarchy using a small 1D yoked surface code as an intermediate tier to cut the expensive yoke-verification latency of 2D yoked surface codes in fault-tolerant quantum architectures.
motivation: In yoked surface code architectures, loading an idle program qubit requires non-fault-tolerant retrieval followed by yoke verification (178 cycles), which dominates memory access latency and can be orders of magnitude slower than the 8-cycle retrieval.
method: The authors add an L1 tier of 1D yoked surface codes, which are less storage-efficient but have negligible verification latency, and design two policies—demand-driven (Trident-D) and prefetch-driven (Trident-P)—to route most loads to L1 instead of the 2D YSC L2 tier.
result: Trident-D and Trident-P achieve reported speedups over the two-level baseline while increasing the physical qubit cost of memory by only 4.9%.
conclusion: A modest intermediate 1D YSC tier can substantially reduce verification overhead of 2D YSCs, offering a favorable speedup-versus-qubit-cost tradeoff for FTQC memory hierarchies.

title: Single-step Su(3) Hahn Echo In A Qutrit Atom Interferometer
authors: Chirantan Mitra, Lucas Gabardos, Fran\c{c}ois Impens, David Gu\'ery-Odelin, David Wilkowski, Chang Chi Kwong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32160v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Hahn echo is a well-known dynamical decoupling method that refocuses the dephasing due to energy inhomogeneities of a spin-1/2 ensemble and is widely used to extend phase coherence in quantum computers and sensors. Extensions of such techniques beyond the spin-1/2 have been reported, but have mainly used SU(2) gates, limiting their scalability. Here, we generalize the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) gates and extend the coherence time by more than an order of magnitude. The gates are generated through optimal control theory and implemented in an ultracold atomic ensemble in free fall. A quantum process tomography procedure benchmarks the gates and yields fidelities of ~ 93%, limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors. Due to the geometry of the laser beams, the generalized Hahn echo also realizes a three-path Mach-Zehnder atomic interferometer with two independent interferometric phase differences. Our results therefore establish SU(3) control for dynamical decoupling of qutrits and multi-path atom interferometers, with the latter opening the possibility for vector force measurements and interferometric tests of the validity of Born's rule.
tldr: The paper generalizes the Hahn echo to qutrits using single-step SU(3) optimal-control gates in an ultracold atom interferometer, extending coherence and enabling multi-path interferometry.
motivation: Dynamical decoupling beyond spin-1/2 typically relies on SU(2) gate decompositions, limiting scalability; this work aims to exploit direct SU(3) control of qutrits for coherence extension and multi-path sensing.
method: Optimal control theory generates SU(3) gates implemented in a free-falling ultracold atomic ensemble, with quantum process tomography used to benchmark gate performance and a three-path Mach-Zehnder geometry arising from the laser configuration.
result: The qutrit Hahn echo extends coherence time by more than an order of magnitude, achieves gate fidelities of about 93% limited mainly by state preparation and measurement errors, and realizes a three-path interferometer with two independent phase differences.
conclusion: The results establish SU(3) control for qutrit dynamical decoupling and multi-path atom interferometry, with potential applications in vector force measurements and interferometric tests of Born's rule.

title: Demonstrating RFSoC-based Control Of A Fully Connected Exchange-Only Qubit
authors: Abigail L. Wessels, M. Garrett Bimstefer, Joseph D. Broz, Alen Senanian, Andrew E. Oriani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Semiconductor triple-quantum dots (TQDs) are a promising platform for scalable quantum information processing, but the community has so far lacked access to affordable and flexible high-speed control electronics. SpinQICK, an open-source spin qubit-control package built on the Xilinx Radio Frequency System-on-Chip (RFSoC), directly addresses this gap by leveraging the high sampling-rate signal generation and advanced digital signal processing (DSP) capabilities of the Quantum Instrumentation Control Kit (QICK) to enable precise time-domain voltage control and readout of semiconductor spin qubits. In this paper, we use spinQICK to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only device. We also introduce and experimentally verify a novel dynamical decoupling (DD) sequence enabled by the triangular TQD and leverage its unique decoupling properties to characterize electrical noise. These results establish spinQICK as a low-cost, flexible platform for semiconductor spin qubit control and provide a pathway for hardware optimization through qubit-level noise diagnostics.
tldr: The authors use the open-source spinQICK RFSoC control stack to demonstrate coherent control, state preparation, and readout of a fully connected triangular exchange-only triple quantum dot, and introduce a device-specific dynamical decoupling sequence for electrical noise spectroscopy.
motivation: Semiconductor triple quantum dots are a promising scalable spin-qubit platform, but progress has been limited by the cost and inflexibility of high-speed control electronics; an affordable, open, FPGA/RFSoC-based control layer is needed.
method: An RFSoC-based control package (spinQICK, built on QICK) provides time-domain voltage control and readout of a triangular exchange-only TQD; standard coherent-control and readout protocols are implemented, and a new dynamical decoupling sequence exploiting the triangle's full connectivity is designed and tested as a noise diagnostic.
result: Coherent control, state preparation, and readout of the fully connected exchange-only device are demonstrated, and the triangular DD sequence is experimentally verified to reveal electrical noise characteristics of the device.
conclusion: spinQICK is established as a low-cost, flexible control platform for semiconductor spin qubits, and qubit-level noise diagnostics via tailored DD sequences offer a practical route to hardware optimization.

The pseudospectra connection may interest researchers in spectral theory and non-Hermitian quantum mechanics. The C*-algebra approach is also pertinent to algebraic quantum field theory and quantum statistical mechanics.
deep_read.overall_assessment: The paper offers a significant mathematical contribution by generalizing uncertainty relations to multiple observables in a C*-algebraic setting and introducing a novel link to pseudospectra. While the results are rigorous and elegant, the lack of concrete examples and the abstract nature may limit immediate physical applicability. The work is likely of high quality and novelty for mathematically inclined quantum physicists, but its impact could be enhanced by demonstrating tightness and applications in specific quantum systems.

title: Asymptotic Scars Arising From The Remnants Of Quantum Phase Transitions
authors: Leonard Logari\'c, Shane Dooley, Tsuyoshi Okubo, Nobuyuki Yoshioka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32037v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Many-body localisation, Hilbert space fragmentation and quantum many-body scars (QMBS) are well-established mechanisms of ergodicity breaking in quantum systems. Recently, asymptotic quantum many-body scars (AQMBS), non-thermal states whose stability grows with system size, have been proposed theoretically and probed experimentally. Here, we show that AQMBS arise naturally as remnants of certain quantum phase transitions. For a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians, we prove that their gapless excitations survive deformation into a scarred Hamiltonian as states whose energy variance is bounded by the excitation gap. Consequently, the gapless excitations at a quantum critical point become AQMBS of the scarred Hamiltonian. Their fidelity relaxation time is then set by the critical scaling of the gap, determined by the dynamic critical exponent. Modelling the critical Fredkin and Motzkin chains and the two-dimensional PVBS model, we obtain AQMBS whose variances directly reflect the dynamic exponents of the underlying transitions. Where the gap of the Motzkin chain closes super-exponentially, we find exponentially stable AQMBS, for which we also observe numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement.
tldr: The paper shows that asymptotic quantum many-body scars can arise as remnants of gapless excitations at quantum phase transitions in frustration-free Hamiltonians.
motivation: Quantum many-body scars are an important mechanism of ergodicity breaking, and understanding their origin and stability is a central problem in quantum many-body dynamics.
method: The authors prove that gapless excitations of a broad class of frustration-free Hamiltonians survive deformation into scarred Hamiltonians, with energy variance bounded by the excitation gap, and model critical Fredkin, Motzkin, and 2D PVBS chains.
result: The resulting asymptotic scars have relaxation times set by critical scaling and dynamic critical exponents; in the Motzkin chain, super-exponential gap closing yields exponentially stable scars with numerical evidence of volume-law entanglement.
conclusion: Quantum phase transitions can naturally generate asymptotically stable scar states, linking critical scaling to non-thermal eigenstate properties and long-lived dynamics.

title: Performing A Quantum Subroutine Using Cluster States
authors: Sakibul Islam Rayhan, Karima Hassan, Md Rasedujjaman, Md Mohsinur Rahman Adnan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32227v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum subroutines, like their classical counterparts, serve as essential components of larger algorithms. They can be realized using gate based architectures or measurement based quantum computation (MBQC), where computation proceeds through adaptive measurements on highly entangled cluster states. In this work, we implement a phase oracle as a reusable subroutine within the MBQC framework using experimentally feasible cluster states. Unlike prior demonstrations of Grover's algorithm in MBQC that omit explicit oracle construction, our approach provides a transparent formulation of the oracle subroutine, including its measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding MBQC measurement circuits.
tldr: The paper implements a reusable phase-oracle subroutine for Grover's algorithm within measurement-based quantum computation using experimentally feasible cluster states.
motivation: Quantum subroutines are essential building blocks for larger algorithms, and MBQC offers a measurement-driven alternative to gate-based architectures; prior MBQC Grover demonstrations often omit explicit oracle construction.
method: The authors formulate a phase oracle as an MBQC subroutine, specifying measurement patterns, byproduct correlations, density-matrix simulations, and corresponding measurement circuits on cluster states.
result: They provide a transparent construction of the oracle subroutine and simulate its behavior, showing how adaptive measurements and byproduct corrections realize the desired phase-oracle action.
conclusion: The work offers a practical MBQC implementation template for oracle-based subroutines, though its contribution is primarily architectural and demonstrative rather than information-theoretic.

title: Positive Planar Measures For Spectral Pinching And The Corrected Bmv Conjecture
authors: Trung Hoa Dinh, Cong Trinh Le, Trung Dung Vuong
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31851v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We prove the corrected Bessis--Moussa--Villani pinching conjecture for all symmetrized word averages. For Hermitian matrices [MATH] and [MATH], we construct a positive compactly supported measure [MATH] on [MATH] such that \[ \Tr f(xA+yB)-\Tr f(xA+yD) =y^2\int_{\mathbb R^2}f''(xa+yb)\,d\zeta_{A,B}(a,b). \] Its total mass is [MATH]. This representation proves the corrected conjecture, including its equality cases, and gives a positive bivariate moment representation for the coefficient differences. We also derive complete monotonicity of normalized exponential pinching defects and a comparison with Lie--Trotter approximations. A one-dimensional second-order loss measure is obtained for trace-preserving conditional expectations on finite tracial von Neumann algebras. Finally, we relate [MATH] to Hein\"avaara's tracial joint spectral measure by an explicit positive radial transform.
tldr: The paper proves a corrected Bessis--Moussa--Villani pinching conjecture using positive planar measures and derives trace-function representations for matrix and von Neumann algebra settings.
motivation: BMV-type conjectures concern positivity properties of traces of matrix functions and spectral pinching, and a corrected version requires a rigorous positive-measure representation.
method: The authors construct a positive compactly supported bivariate measure for Hermitian matrices such that a trace difference is represented by a second-derivative integral, and relate it to tracial joint spectral measures.
result: They establish the corrected conjecture including equality cases, obtain complete monotonicity of normalized exponential pinching defects, compare with Lie--Trotter approximations, and derive a one-dimensional loss measure for trace-preserving conditional expectations.
conclusion: The work provides a positive-measure framework for spectral pinching and trace inequalities, with connections to tracial joint spectral measures in finite von Neumann algebras.

title: Quantum Cryptomania With Classical Communication Without One-Way Functions
authors: Amit Behera Mohammed Barhoush
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32145v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In classical cryptography, one-way functions are necessary for most of cryptography. In the quantum world, however, Kretschmer at {TQC'21} and subsequent works have demonstrated that quantum versions of various primitives in minicrypt, such as signatures and private-key encryption, do not require quantum-computable one-way functions (s). However, the question of the necessity of s for primitives in Cryptomania like public-key encryption with classical public keys and ciphertexts () has remained open. We provide a comprehensive picture of the relationship between and . First, our main result is a black-box separation between s and . In particular, we show that relative to a unitary, real, and self-inverse oracle, there exists a scheme (with classical keys and ciphertexts), but s do not exist. Further, our oracles admit a point-function obfuscation construction, thus ruling out black-box construction of from point function obfuscations. On the positive side, we construct from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits with classical obfuscated descriptions and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles, which is known to be a potentially weaker assumption than s, due to an existing black-box separation. Our construction is the quantum analog of the classical construction of from one-way functions and indistinguishability obfuscation in the quantum computation with classical communication (QCCC) setting.
tldr: The paper establishes a black-box separation between quantum public-key encryption and one-way functions, and constructs the former from quantum indistinguishability obfuscation and one-way puzzles.
motivation: Understanding the minimal assumptions required for quantum cryptographic primitives, particularly whether public-key encryption implies one-way functions, is a fundamental question in quantum cryptography.
method: Uses oracle separation techniques with unitary, real, self-inverse oracles to show a black-box separation, and provides a positive construction based on quantum indistinguishability obfuscation for quantum circuits and efficiently verifiable one-way puzzles.
result: Demonstrates that quantum public-key encryption with classical keys and ciphertexts does not imply one-way functions in a black-box sense, and that it can be built from potentially weaker assumptions than one-way functions.
conclusion: This provides a comprehensive picture of the relationship between quantum public-key encryption and one-way functions, advancing the foundations of quantum cryptography.

title: Multiport Photonic Routing With A Single Cavity-based Electro-optic Phase Shifter Per Port
authors: Alessandro Buzzi, Bjarke A. Frederiksen, Dashiell L. P. Vitullo, Mikkel Heuck, Dirk R. Englund
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31757v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Programmable photonic meshes can perform general linear transformations, but universal transformations on [MATH] modes require [MATH] programmable phase shifters, which cannot simultaneously achieve low drive voltage, gigahertz speed, zero static power, lossless modulation, and a compact footprint. Signal routing does not require universal transformations, which allows considerable circuit simplifications. We present a compact reflective circuit architecture that connects all input-output pairs across [MATH] modes in [MATH] steps using only [MATH] programmable phase shifters. The circuit comprises a single passive [MATH] interferometer and a single column of programmable reflective phase shifters. We demonstrate the architecture by implementing a [MATH] router in x-cut thin-film lithium niobate with a passive multimode interferometer and phase shifters based on single-sided photonic-crystal nanobeam cavities. Our programmable devices exhibit a [MATH] GHz/V resonance tuning efficiency via the Pockels effect, a footprint of [MATH], sub-5-V drive voltage, and a 6.2 GHz electro-optic bandwidth. Through voltage-space characterization and physical modeling, we identify routing states with extinction ratios exceeding 11 dB at each output and demonstrate sequential routing at an equipment-limited speed of 10 MHz. Our results establish cavity-enhanced Pockels switching as a routing layer for classical and quantum computing interconnects across visible and near-infrared wavelengths.
tldr: The paper demonstrates a compact programmable photonic routing architecture using cavity-enhanced Pockels phase shifters in thin-film lithium niobate, aimed at classical and quantum computing interconnects.
motivation: Universal programmable photonic meshes require many phase shifters with demanding performance, but signal routing needs only pair-to-pair connectivity, allowing simplified circuits.
method: The authors design a reflective circuit with one passive multimode interferometer and one column of programmable reflective phase shifters, fabricated in x-cut thin-film lithium niobate using photonic-crystal nanobeam cavities.
result: The 4-mode router achieves GHz/V tuning efficiency, sub-5-V drive, 6.2 GHz electro-optic bandwidth, extinction ratios above 11 dB, and sequential routing at 10 MHz.
conclusion: Cavity-enhanced Pockels switching is proposed as a scalable routing layer for classical and quantum computing interconnects across visible and near-infrared wavelengths.

title: The Permutation And Automorphism Groups Of Univariate Multiplicity Codes
authors: Eduardo Camps Moreno, Hiram H. L\'opez, Umberto Mart\'inez-Pe\~{n}as, Rodrigo San-Jos\'e
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We give explicit characterizations of the permutations and linear isometries that leave (univariate) multiplicity codes invariant. We consider any evaluation subset of the finite field, any multiplicity and dimension, and the automorphisms are with respect to the Niederreiter-Rosenblom-Tsfasman (NRT) metric. For multiplicity one, we recover the permutation and automorphism groups of classical Reed--Solomon codes in the classical Hamming metric. In the main dimension range, automorphisms are uniquely determined by a projectivity that permutes the evaluation subset, up to multiplication by a nonzero scalar. For multiplicity one, permutations are given by affine maps that permute the evaluation subset. In contrast, for multiplicity at least two, permutations are only given by translations that permute the evaluation subset. Finally, we give an algebraic characterization of automorphisms of multiplicity codes for the folded Hamming metric.
tldr: The paper characterizes permutation and automorphism groups of univariate multiplicity codes under the NRT metric, generalizing classical Reed-Solomon code symmetries.
motivation: Multiplicity codes are a classical algebraic coding family, and understanding their symmetries is important for code classification and decoding-related structural analysis.
method: The authors explicitly characterize permutations and linear isometries preserving multiplicity codes for arbitrary evaluation subsets, multiplicities, and dimensions, using projectivities and affine/translation maps depending on multiplicity.
result: They show that in the main dimension range automorphisms are determined by projectivities permuting the evaluation subset up to scalar multiplication, and that for multiplicity at least two permutations reduce to translations, while multiplicity one recovers Reed-Solomon behavior.
conclusion: The work provides a complete algebraic description of automorphism groups for univariate multiplicity codes in the NRT metric and for the folded Hamming metric.

title: Polarization On Bounded Euclidean Spaces And More General Compact Groups
authors: Sharang M. Sriramu, Lampros Gavalakis, Ioannis Kontoyiannis, Aaron B. Wagner
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32760v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We establish polarization for memoryless sources taking values on the unit-perimeter circle, or on more general compact groups, under Ar{\i}kan's polar transform. For sources with finite differential entropy, all but an [MATH] fraction of the conditional differential entropies in successive cancellation order lie within any fixed positive distance of zero, where [MATH] is the block length. Examples indicate that the true polarization rate is indeed very slow: an inverse-logarithmic rate does not underestimate the polarization speed at moderate block lengths.
tldr: This paper proves polarization of memoryless sources on compact groups under Arıkan's polar transform and shows that the polarization rate can be very slow.
motivation: Polar codes rely on channel polarization, but polarization behavior for sources on continuous bounded spaces and general compact groups is less understood.
method: The authors analyze the Arıkan polar transform for memoryless sources taking values on the unit-perimeter circle or more general compact groups, focusing on conditional differential entropies in successive-cancellation order.
result: For sources with finite differential entropy, all but a vanishing fraction of conditional differential entropies lie arbitrarily close to zero, and examples suggest an inverse-logarithmic polarization rate at moderate block lengths.
conclusion: The work extends polarization theory beyond standard discrete or real-valued settings, but it is a classical coding/information-theory contribution with no direct quantum information component.

title: Encoding-Sensitive Nullstellensatz Certificates For Syndrome Exclusion In Ldpc Codes: Sharp Local Bounds And A Linear Separation
authors: Malihe Aliasgari, Hassan Khodaiemehr, Khadijeh Bagheri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32171v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Certifying that a parity-check matrix has no nonempty set of at most t variable nodes leaving at most b checks unsatisfied arises in minimum-distance and trapping-set analysis. Such absence is the infeasibility of a polynomial system, provable by an independently checkable Nullstellensatz certificate. The degree of these certificates depends strongly on how the two cardinality constraints are encoded, although the encodings have identical solutions. For a local encoding with inclusion-exclusion and cardinality obstructions, we construct explicit certificates of degree at most t + b + K + 1, with K logarithmic in the maximum check degree; this bound is independent of the block length and cannot be improved in general. For a standard counting encoding, a generalized planted-knapsack theorem, which pulls back a knapsack functional with an arbitrary target, gives lower bounds linear in the block length for cycle codes, regular codes of girth at least six near the feasibility boundary, array-based quasi-cyclic codes and minimum-distance certificates for arrays of circulant permutation matrices, where the local degree stays bounded. On array codes and regular codes of girth at least eight, planted column pairs extend these bounds to odd column weight with no unsatisfied checks. The planting argument is optimal among such pullbacks. All computed degrees and certificates are verified in exact rational arithmetic; bounds are distinguished from exact minimum degrees. Local certificates for quasi-cyclic matrices, including a lifted fifth-generation New Radio base graph, pass two independent verifiers.
tldr: The paper constructs encoding-dependent Nullstellensatz certificates for syndrome exclusion in classical LDPC codes, proving sharp local degree bounds and a linear separation between encodings.
motivation: Certifying that no small set of variable nodes leaves few checks unsatisfied is important for minimum-distance and trapping-set analysis, but the degree of such certificates depends strongly on how cardinality constraints are encoded.
method: The authors compare a local inclusion-exclusion/cardinality encoding with a standard counting encoding, construct explicit Nullstellensatz certificates, and use planted-knapsack pullbacks to prove lower bounds; all certificates and degrees are verified in exact rational arithmetic.
result: The local encoding gives certificates of degree at most t+b+K+1, independent of block length and tight in general, while the counting encoding yields linear-in-block-length lower bounds for cycle codes, regular girth-at-least-six codes, array-based quasi-cyclic codes, and related minimum-distance certificates.
conclusion: Encoding choice critically affects certificate complexity for LDPC syndrome exclusion, with local encodings enabling length-independent certificates and counting encodings suffering linear lower bounds; the results are classical coding-theoretic with no direct quantum extension.

title: QuantumMatterExplorer: An Autonomous Agent For The Discovery Of Quantum Many-Body Phases Of Matter
authors: Jannes Nys, Andrew Jreissaty, Juan Carrasquilla
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32001v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Mapping the phase diagram of a new quantum Hamiltonian demands expert judgement at every step: which observables to measure, where in parameter space to compute, or how to separate genuine order from finite-size artefacts. We introduce QuantumMatterExplorer, an autonomous agent that takes only a Hamiltonian and its parameter ranges as input and returns a phase diagram obtained from its own numerical simulations. The agent is built on a large language model and is designed to reason over a long horizon, maintain a persistent written plan, and drive a set of computational tools, with density-matrix renormalization group (DMRG) calculations cross-checked against independent exact diagonalization. The agent combines a large language model with persistent planning, a library of expert computational-physics skills, and density-matrix renormalization group calculations validated against independent exact diagonalization. It adaptively selects quantities to evaluate, refines parameter scans, and performs finite-size analyses as evidence accumulates. After validating the approach on Hamiltonians with known transitions, we challenge it with a frustrated bilinear-biquadratic spin-1 chain with single-ion anisotropy, whose two-dimensional phase diagram was published only recently and is unlikely to appear in any training corpus. Given no hint about the expected physics, the agent proposes which observables to probe, and identifies candidate N\'eel, Haldane and dimerized phases, in broad agreement with the reference phase diagram. It also detects incommensurate correlations and infers the frustration-dependent geometry of the phase boundaries, all within an eight-hour compute budget. These results open a practical route to the autonomous computational discovery of new phases of quantum matter.
tldr: QuantumMatterExplorer is an LLM-based autonomous agent that plans and executes DMRG/ED simulations to map quantum many-body phase diagrams with minimal human input.
motivation: Determining phase diagrams of new quantum Hamiltonians requires continual expert judgement about observables, scan regions, and finite-size effects, which the authors aim to automate.
method: The agent couples a large language model with persistent written planning, a library of expert computational-physics skills, and DMRG calculations cross-checked against exact diagonalization, adaptively refining parameter scans and finite-size analyses.
