method: The authors run pre-registered adversarial tests on multiple guard models, introduce the GuardRebind benchmark, analyze attack families per guard, and evaluate a training mitigation that scores content by its most harmful part.
result: An appended forged query plus decoy bypasses all 75 held-out AdvBench requests flagged by Shieldstral-1.0-3B, and each of five guards has an attack family clearing at least 93% of flagged items; the proposed training mitigation reduces attack success to 0.8-1.6% on held-out attack families but remains vulnerable to score-guided search.
conclusion: Target rebinding reveals a structural vulnerability in LLM safety guards, and although harm-aware training substantially improves robustness, adaptive search can still find bypasses, indicating an ongoing adversarial arms race.

title: Omni-UBench: Benchmarking Omni-Modal LLM-based Guardrails Across Safety, Utility, And Reliability
authors: Junhao Wang, Yidou Chen, Li Lu, Hongwei Yao, Xiaodan Li, Mengjie Wu, Yuefeng Chen, Zhan Qin, Kui Ren
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31713v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advances in Omni-modal Large Language Models (OLLMs) have enabled increasingly seamless human-AI interaction, but their unified processing of heterogeneous modalities also expands the attack surface, allowing adversaries to exploit richer input compositions to circumvent safety alignment. To counter such risks, omni-modal guardrails have been proposed to detect and filter unsafe queries across arbitrary modalities. However, their capabilities and limitations remain insufficiently understood due to the absence of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark. In this paper, we present Omni-UBench, the first comprehensive framework for omni-modal safety assessment, evaluating guardrail models along three critical dimensions, i.e., safety, utility, and reliability. Omni-UBench curates over 183k samples drawn from 35+ heterogeneous sources spanning text, image, audio, video, and their cross-modal combinations, annotated with safety labels under a unified risk taxonomy. Benchmarking under Omni-UBench on 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails yields several key findings, including: (1) modern OLLMs exhibit strong content moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; (2) existing guardrails still struggle to identify cross-modal queries that conceal harmful intent or involve sophisticated jailbreaks; (3) they further exhibit substantial safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns, revealing a deficient understanding of cross-modal safety semantics. Our findings provide valuable insights for developing more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.
tldr: Omni-UBench is the first comprehensive benchmark for evaluating omni-modal LLM-based guardrails across safety, utility, and reliability dimensions, spanning over 183k samples from 35+ heterogeneous multimodal sources.
motivation: Omni-modal LLMs unify text, image, audio, and video processing, expanding the attack surface for adversarial misuse, yet the capabilities and limitations of omni-modal guardrails remain poorly understood due to the lack of a comprehensive evaluation benchmark.
method: The authors curate 183k+ annotated samples from 35+ sources covering five modality configurations, define a unified risk taxonomy, and benchmark 15 representative OLLMs and omni-modal guardrails along safety, utility, and reliability axes.
result: Modern OLLMs show strong content-moderation potential even without guardrail-specific tuning; existing guardrails still fail on cross-modal queries hiding harmful intent or sophisticated jailbreaks, and exhibit safety hallucination and over-sensitivity to textual patterns.
conclusion: The findings expose deficient cross-modal safety semantics understanding in current guardrails and provide guidance for building more trustworthy omni-modal guardrails in future research.

title: Two-colour Crossing Minimization In Complete Geometric Graphs Is NP-hard
authors: Zhe Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31719v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Given a fixed straight-line drawing of a complete graph, we seek a two-colouring of its edges that minimizes the number of monochromatic crossing pairs. We prove that the threshold decision problem is NP-complete, even when the vertices are in general position and have integer coordinates of polynomial binary length. Thus exact minimization is NP-hard, answering the complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019. The reduction is from MaxCut on permutation graphs. Its main difficulty is to control the edges required by completeness, whose colours must remain free. We construct a large comparison grid with two stable colour phases and use additional points to assign costs to the edges that encode the source graph. A geometric separation eliminates one large class of unwanted crossings. The costs of all remaining edges are included in a computable baseline and bounded errors, with each unit of the source objective amplified beyond the total error. The construction is deterministic and has polynomial size and coordinate bit length.
tldr: The paper proves that two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs is NP-hard.
motivation: It resolves a complexity question posed at the Crossing Number Workshop in 2019 concerning edge-colourings that minimize monochromatic crossing pairs.
method: The author gives a polynomial-time reduction from MaxCut on permutation graphs, using a comparison grid and geometric separation to control crossing costs.
result: The threshold decision problem is shown to be NP-complete, even for general-position vertices with polynomially bounded integer coordinates, implying NP-hardness of exact minimization.
conclusion: The work settles the computational complexity of two-colour crossing minimization in complete geometric graphs and provides a deterministic polynomial-size construction.

title: Ulysses: A Security Harness For Synthesizing Verifiable Web Exploits
authors: Aditya Oke, Andr\'e Vicente Duarte, Rui Melo, Shubham Gandhi, Nachiket Kotalwar, Charmi Khandor, Danqing Wang, Carolyn Ros\'e, Lei Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31831v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How can an AI agent automatically discover security vulnerabilities in any software repository? Existing approaches use LLMs to generate software vulnerability exploits. However, it is challenging for an LLM to reliably verify its own generated exploits. In this paper, we propose Ulysses, a multi-agent security harness to synthesize verifiable vulnerability exploits for web applications. Ulysses converts candidate vulnerability findings into verified Proofs of Exploitability by iteratively exploring exploit hypotheses and establishing success in independently observed execution effects. We evaluated Ulysses on WebExploitGym, a curated benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications that span 5 languages and 7 frameworks. Ulysses produces verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories. It also discovered 4 new proofs of exploitability that have never been previously reported.
tldr: Ulysses is a multi-agent LLM harness that turns candidate web vulnerability findings into verified proofs of exploitability by iteratively testing exploit hypotheses against independently observed execution effects.
motivation: LLMs can generate exploit candidates but cannot reliably verify their own outputs, so automated vulnerability discovery lacks trustworthy validation of generated exploits.
method: A multi-agent security harness that iteratively explores exploit hypotheses and confirms success through independently observed execution effects, evaluated on WebExploitGym, a benchmark of exploitable instances from 25 real-world web applications across 5 languages and 7 frameworks.
result: Ulysses produced verified proofs for 10 of 25 real-world advisories and discovered 4 previously unreported proofs of exploitability.
conclusion: Structured multi-agent verification improves the reliability of LLM-driven exploit synthesis, though coverage of real-world advisories remains partial.

title: Not An Accident: Exploiting Safety Filter Inadequacy In Humanoid Robots
authors: Tiffany Bao, Shangtao Li, Yifan Sun, Mengwen He, Bowei Li, Alden Wang, Changliu Liu, Ruoyu Wang, David Brumley
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31923v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As humanoid robots move from research laboratories toward deployment in human-centered environments such as homes, hospitals, and warehouses, safe operation around nearby people and objects becomes a fundamental requirement. Safety filters have emerged as a promising technique to address this challenge by providing mathematical guarantees that generated control actions do not result in collisions. This paper shows that these guarantees hold only when the safety parameters are configured correctly. However, correct parameter configurations are task- and environment-specific, and no general method exists to determine them across diverse deployments. As a result, safety filters shipped with humanoid robots can fail after deployment in specific scenarios. We show that attackers can exploit these failures through only normal user interactions without any additional privileges or capabilities. To demonstrate this risk, we present goal insertion attacks and develop SIREN, an automated tool that identifies vulnerable inserting goals for a given task and environment. Experimental results show that SIREN identifies attacks in all vulnerable scenarios in the SPARK dataset. Compared with a baseline approach, SIREN discovers three times as many attacks. We also show that SIREN is able to generate attacks against a real humanoid and cause it to collide while executing tasks. These results demonstrate that current safety filters introduce exploitable vulnerabilities that can cause safety violations, which reveals that existing safety mechanisms can themselves become a source of safety risk for humanoid robots.
tldr: The paper shows that safety filters in humanoid robots are only valid under correctly configured, task-specific safety parameters, and demonstrates automated goal-insertion attacks (SIREN) that exploit misconfigurations through ordinary user interaction to cause collisions.
motivation: As humanoid robots enter human-centered environments, safety filters are relied upon to guarantee collision-free control, but their correctness depends on environment- and task-specific parameter choices for which no general determination method exists, leaving deployed systems vulnerable.
method: The authors formalize goal insertion attacks available to unprivileged users and build SIREN, an automated tool that searches for vulnerable inserted goals given a task and environment, evaluated on the SPARK dataset and against a real humanoid robot.
result: SIREN finds attacks in all vulnerable scenarios of the SPARK dataset, discovers three times as many attacks as a baseline, and successfully induces collisions in a physical humanoid robot executing tasks.
conclusion: Current safety filters can themselves become a source of safety risk for humanoid robots, motivating configuration-robust or verifiably correct safety mechanisms.

title: Differentiable Combinatorial Auction Design: Optimizing Revenue-Welfare-Fairness Frontiers With Graph Attention Networks
authors: Mai Pham, Vikrant Vaze, Peter Chin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31977v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing optimal auctions for allocating public infrastructure-such as airport slots and energy resources-is challenging due to interdependent resources and complex side-constraints. While the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves (VCG) auction guarantees maximum welfare, it cannot maximize revenue or accommodate the multi-objective trade-offs inherent in public infrastructure systems. We propose a differentiable, constraint-aware framework for combinatorial auction design that enables end-to-end learning of fractionally feasible, approximately strategy-proof mechanisms. Our primary contribution is a combinatorial constraint enforcement technique that ensures fractional feasibility by construction, bypassing the need for penalty-based approximations. We introduce CAGraph, a novel graph-based architecture designed to capture dependencies between items and bidders, alongside CANet and CAFormer as deep learning baselines, for combinatorial settings. We also provide a Matching Pursuit-inspired decomposition that maps fractional allocations to feasible discrete allocations and empirically evaluates the resulting discretization gap. In synthetic benchmarks and an airport slot-divestiture case study, respectively, the learned mechanisms achieve up to 73.5% and 180% higher expected revenue than VCG, under small empirical regret. Finally, we visualize the Pareto frontiers for revenue, welfare, and fairness, providing regulators with a decision-support tool to design infrastructure auctions that balance profitability, efficiency and equity.
tldr: The paper proposes a differentiable, constraint-aware deep learning framework (with a graph attention architecture, CAGraph) for designing combinatorial auctions that trade off revenue, welfare, and fairness for public infrastructure allocation.
motivation: VCG auctions maximize welfare but cannot optimize revenue or handle the multi-objective trade-offs and side constraints needed when allocating interdependent public infrastructure such as airport slots and energy resources.
method: The authors build an end-to-end differentiable mechanism design pipeline with a by-construction fractional feasibility constraint enforcement technique, introduce CAGraph (plus CANet and CAFormer baselines) to model item-bidder dependencies, and use a Matching Pursuit-inspired rounding scheme to obtain discrete feasible allocations.
result: On synthetic benchmarks and an airport slot-divestiture case study, the learned mechanisms achieve up to 73.5% and 180% higher expected revenue than VCG with small empirical regret, and Pareto frontiers for revenue, welfare, and fairness are visualized.
conclusion: Differentiable graph-based auction design can provide regulators with a decision-support tool for balancing profitability, efficiency, and equity in infrastructure auctions.

title: Wade: An LSTM-Based Anomaly Detection Engine For WebAssembly Applications
authors: Ilaria Campestrini, Stefano Zanero, Engin Kirda
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: WebAssembly (Wasm) enables near-native performance for web applications through a portable and sandboxed execution model. However, its limited runtime protection mechanisms (e.g., the lack of stack canaries and address space layout randomization (ASLR)) leave Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks. We present WADE (WebAssembly Anomaly Detection Engine), a system that detects anomalous runtime behaviors in browser-executed WebAssembly applications. WADE monitors function-level execution traces collected under benign conditions and trains a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) network to learn the normal execution behavior of each application. At runtime, the model flags deviations from these learned patterns as potential attacks. Unlike signature-based approaches, WADE builds application-specific behavioral models, enabling detection of both known and previously unseen attacks without per-vulnerability signatures. We evaluate WADE on a dataset of 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, achieving zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.
tldr: WADE is an LSTM-based anomaly detection engine that monitors function-level execution traces of WebAssembly applications to flag runtime attacks.
motivation: WebAssembly's sandboxed execution model lacks common runtime protections such as stack canaries and ASLR, making browser-executed Wasm applications vulnerable to traditional attacks.
method: WADE collects benign function-level execution traces, trains an LSTM network to model normal application behavior, and at runtime treats deviations from the learned patterns as potential attacks.
result: Evaluated on 67 WebAssembly applications spanning ten vulnerability classes, WADE achieved zero false negatives and a 0.42% false positive rate.
conclusion: Application-specific behavioral modeling with LSTMs can detect known and previously unseen Wasm attacks without per-vulnerability signatures.

title: Trace: Data-Free Text Reconstruction Attacks Against Approximate Unlearning In LLMs
authors: Mengying Zhang, Derui Wang, Ibrahim Khalil, Bowen Liu, Xiaoyu Xia, Minhui Xue
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31995v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As large language models (LLMs) face growing demands for data removal driven by regulatory compliance, copyright concerns, and privacy protection, approximate unlearning has emerged as a practical alternative to expensive full retraining. In practice, pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots are often maintained for auditing and rollback, introducing a previously overlooked side channel. This paper demonstrates that approximate unlearning in LLM can leave residual traces within model snapshots, which may be recoverable and thus enable the privacy breaches that approximate unlearning is intended to prevent. Here, we propose TRACE, a framework that reconstructs unlearned training data given access to pre- and post-unlearning model snapshots, without any data-specific prior knowledge. To achieve this, TRACE identifies a compact set of candidate tokens from embedding-level parameter differences to constrain the search space, and assembles sequences via a contrastive scoring mechanism based on the perplexity gap between the two models. A two-stage exploration-then-completion strategy enables the recovery of multiple distinct samples. Extensive experiments on various datasets, including TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP, across multiple LLMs and six representative unlearning methods, demonstrate that TRACE achieves high-fidelity reconstruction. This paper exposes significant privacy risks in current LLM approximate unlearning deployments and highlights the need for defenses against parameter-difference leakage and appropriate management of model snapshot access.
tldr: TRACE reconstructs supposedly unlearned training data from paired pre- and post-unlearning LLM snapshots without any data-specific priors.
motivation: Approximate unlearning is widely deployed for regulatory and privacy compliance, yet pre/post-unlearning model snapshots retained for auditing may leak residual information about the data that was meant to be removed.
method: The framework narrows the token search space using embedding-level parameter differences between the two snapshots, then assembles candidate sequences via a contrastive perplexity-gap scoring mechanism with an explore-then-complete two-stage strategy to recover multiple distinct samples.
result: Experiments on TOFU, MUSE, and WMDP across several LLMs and six unlearning methods show high-fidelity reconstruction of unlearned data, exposing a parameter-difference side channel.
conclusion: Current approximate unlearning deployments carry significant privacy risks, motivating defenses against parameter-difference leakage and stricter control of model snapshot access.

title: The 3ds Oracle: Bin Attack Via The Network
authors: Suprava Saha Dibya Wasif Faisal (BRAC University)
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32206v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: EMV 3-D Secure (3DS) requires a client-visible continuation boundary in browser-mediated flows; in some deployments, that boundary exposes a pre-authorization classification channel. This paper studies 3DS as a protocol, integration surface, and governance problem, combining standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history, and a bounded live evaluation. We show that client-visible integrations can reflect routing and authentication state before financial authorization, allowing 3DS to function as a profiling and screening channel for issuer controls and cardholder/account state rather than only as a defense. In the tested browser-channel Braintree/Cardinal path, the first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchor cards from bounded adjacent same-range comparison PANs in six of seven distinct ACS/card-range cohorts; separate public evidence, including openly accessible attacker tooling, rotating-proxy support, and illicit paid 3DS card-testing services, shows that comparable signals are already operationalized in the wild. Our live study was deliberately bounded for ethical reasons, so the empirical ceiling reported here reflects researcher restraint rather than an attacker-side scalability limit, although we do not claim network-wide prevalence or candidate issuance. The deeper issue is systemic: decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-boundary assumptions, identifier-linked routing invariants, and fragmented accountability let the exposure persist even when individual actors appear locally conformant. Meaningful remediation therefore requires consortium-level reform, including stricter minimization of client-visible pre-authorization responses, more uniform continuation behavior, and stronger client authenticity and session binding.
tldr: The paper analyzes EMV 3-D Secure payment flows and shows that client-visible pre-authorization responses can act as a profiling and card-testing oracle, which attacker tooling already exploits.
motivation: 3DS is meant to be a fraud defense, but its client-visible continuation boundary may leak routing and authentication state before financial authorization, creating a screening channel for attackers.
method: Combines standards analysis, architectural reconstruction, formal modeling, a documentation audit, disclosure history review, and a deliberately bounded live evaluation on a Braintree/Cardinal browser path comparing anchor cards against same-range PANs across ACS/card-range cohorts.
result: The first client-visible result separated researcher-owned anchors from adjacent same-range PANs in six of seven cohorts, and public evidence shows rotating-proxy tooling and paid 3DS card-testing services already operationalize comparable signals.
conclusion: The exposure is systemic, stemming from decoupled pre-authorization authentication, weak requestor-boundary assumptions, and fragmented accountability, and remediation requires consortium-level reform in response minimization, continuation uniformity, and client authenticity/session binding.

title: Tracing Money Laundering Across DeFi, Bridges, And Mixers On Ethereum
authors: Huan Xing, Gaohe Jin, Bang Fu, Yue Li, Baoning Niu, Xing Fan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32210v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Illicit actors exploit Ethereum's deep liquidity and diverse on-chain services to launder criminal proceeds by combining decentralized finance (DeFi) protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers in multi-stage processes. Existing anti-money laundering tracing methods fail to disentangle the underlying asset-flow paths in complex transactions, potentially misdirecting subsequent tracing; cannot identify cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge information; and treat mixers as generic exit services, overlooking post-mixer laundering flows. We present FPTracer, a framework for tracing illicit assets across Ethereum services. First, we propose a method based on the Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to recover intra-transaction asset-flow paths, which guide accurate tracing and service analysis. Second, we extract discriminative features from asset-flow and execution-evidence perspectives and train a classifier to identify transactions with cross-chain intent. Third, we leverage evidence from the upstream laundering network to analyze potential post-mixer laundering activities. Evaluation on 20 real-world laundering cases demonstrates FPTracer's effectiveness. It achieves the highest recall for both known laundering addresses (98.6%) and destinations (94.2%). It identifies all known uses of bridges in these cases and uncovers 30 previously unreported ones. Among 18 cases with identified Tornado Cash usage, FPTracer can identify potential withdrawal-side activities, which are corroborated by public reports where available.
tldr: FPTracer is a blockchain-forensics framework that traces illicit asset flows across Ethereum DeFi protocols, cross-chain bridges, and mixers to support anti-money-laundering investigations.
motivation: Illicit actors chain DeFi, bridges, and mixers into multi-stage laundering pipelines, and existing AML tracing tools fail to disentangle intra-transaction asset-flow paths, cannot infer cross-chain intent, and treat mixers as terminal exit points.
method: The authors build a Context-Aware Transfer Tree (CATT) to reconstruct intra-transaction asset-flow paths, train a classifier on asset-flow and execution-evidence features to detect cross-chain intent without pre-collected bridge data, and use upstream network evidence to infer post-mixer withdrawal activity.
result: Across 20 real-world cases FPTracer reaches 98.6% recall on known laundering addresses and 94.2% on destinations, recovers all known bridge uses plus 30 previously unreported ones, and surfaces post-mixer withdrawal-side activity in 18 Tornado Cash cases.
conclusion: The work offers a practical blockchain-forensics pipeline for AML tracing, but its contribution is in cryptocurrency security and data mining rather than quantum information science.

title: Beyond Copying: Lifelong Smart Contract Security Task Construction Via Protocol Mutation
authors: Zifan Peng, Peng Huang, Jingyi Zheng, Yingjie Xue, Xuechao Wang, Xinlei He, Xia Hu, Dongrui Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32453v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: AI agents can inspect code and run tests to support smart contract security. SlowMist reports about $38.6 billion in losses across the broader blockchain ecosystem. Existing evaluations can reward memorized or copied answers, including attack code recovered from public blockchain transactions. Reconstructing contracts and validating tasks also require costly manual effort. To address these issues, we propose CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework for lifelong construction of smart contract security tasks via protocol mutation. It automates local contract reconstruction and uses attack execution to select changes to the required calls or inputs. Execution checks guide revisions that make the original attack fail while preserving exploitability, the security objective, and normal functionality. New incidents and audit findings enter the same procedure. With CONSTRAINTDIAL, we construct 3,045 task inputs from 203 public cases, covering detect, exploit, and patch. Compared with reconstruction alone, protocol mutation reduces success with supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average across detect, exploit, and patch. The fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers falls by 9.3 points.
tldr: The paper introduces CONSTRAINTDIAL, a framework that automatically constructs smart-contract security tasks via protocol mutation to prevent AI agents from solving them by copying public attack code.
motivation: Existing smart-contract security benchmarks can reward memorized or copied answers from public blockchain transactions, and manually reconstructing and validating tasks is costly.
method: CONSTRAINTDIAL performs local contract reconstruction and uses attack-execution feedback to mutate required calls or inputs, selecting changes that make original attacks fail while preserving exploitability, security objectives, and normal functionality.
result: Using 203 public cases, the authors construct 3,045 detect/exploit/patch tasks; protocol mutation reduces success from supplied public answers by 10.9 percentage points on average and lowers the fraction of tasks solved by copying online answers by 9.3 points.
conclusion: Protocol mutation can produce lifelong, non-copyable smart-contract security tasks, improving evaluation robustness for AI agents in blockchain security.

title: StarRTT: An End-to-End Real-Time Framework For Blind Zone-Free Rtt Prediction In Starlink Leo Satellite Networks
authors: Jaeyong Lee, Seongjin Jeong, Yusang Park, Hyunho Hwang, Sangmin Han, Wonjae Shin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32540v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Low Earth Orbit (LEO) satellite mega-constellations such as Starlink require frequent handovers due to high orbital velocities, resulting in substantial Round-Trip Time (RTT) fluctuations. Accurate RTT prediction can mitigate these fluctuations, yet it fundamentally relies on continuously updated serving- satellite information. Existing serving-satellite identification methods typically complete identification only at the end of each scheduling cycle, creating an identification blind zone that limits real-time prediction. To overcome this limitation, we develop StarRTT, an end-to-end real-time framework that eliminates the blind zone by integrating per-second serving-satellite identification with RTT prediction. Within this framework, we propose Real-Time Long Short-Term Memory (RT-LSTM), an LSTM-based RTT prediction model designed to capture both non-stationary RTT evolution and time-varying geometric relationships among the serving satellite, user terminal, and gateways. Specifically, a historical LSTM encodes historical RTT observations and real-time serving-satellite and gateway-relative features, while a future LSTM processes Two-Line Element (TLE)-propagated future features of the identified serving satellite up to the next scheduling instant. Under strict real-time back-testing, RT-LSTM achieves a Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 1.405 ms averaged over all 15 prediction horizons and 15 reference time-slot indices, reducing the error by 4.3 %, 11.6 %, and 22.1 % compared with the existing baseline models, LSTM, StarNet, and Attention-based Spatiotemporal Model (ASTM), respectively. Notably, the reduction over LSTM reaches 12.5 % at the scheduling instant, highlighting the benefit of real-time serving-satellite information when recent RTT observations are limited.
tldr: StarRTT is an end-to-end real-time framework that integrates per-second serving-satellite identification with LSTM-based RTT prediction to eliminate the identification blind zone in Starlink LEO networks.
motivation: Frequent handovers in LEO mega-constellations cause large RTT fluctuations, and existing serving-satellite identification only completes at the end of a scheduling cycle, creating a blind zone that prevents real-time RTT prediction.
method: The authors propose RT-LSTM, which uses a historical LSTM over past RTT observations plus real-time serving-satellite and gateway-relative features, and a future LSTM over TLE-propagated features of the identified serving satellite up to the next scheduling instant.
result: Under strict real-time back-testing, RT-LSTM achieves 1.405 ms MAE averaged over 15 horizons and 15 time-slot indices, improving over LSTM, StarNet, and ASTM by 4.3%, 11.6%, and 22.1%, respectively, with a 12.5% gain over LSTM at the scheduling instant.
conclusion: Incorporating real-time serving-satellite information into RTT prediction removes the blind zone and yields consistent accuracy gains, supporting latency mitigation in LEO satellite broadband networks.

title: Capacity Modification For Matching With Couples: An Integer Programming And Computational Study
authors: Zexiao Wu, Genjiu Xu, P\'eter Bir\'o
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32793v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study capacity modification in the Hospitals/Residents problem with Couples, in which hospital capacities and a stable matching are jointly determined. Exact and Cutoff integer programming formulations are developed for the resulting problem. We assume that, for each couple, either both members are matched or neither is. For arbitrary strict preferences, every instance admits a stable matching after changing each hospital capacity by at most two. Total capacity increases by at most one, and this bound is tight. Under sub-responsive and sub-complete couple preferences, a stable matching exists after adding at most one position to each hospital. The total number of additions is at most the number of couples, and this bound is also tight. Computational experiments show that Exact formulations are modestly faster at fixed capacities, whereas Cutoff formulations perform substantially better in the minimum repair experiments and attain higher completion rates in markets with up to 30,000 doctors. Across 96,000 synthetic and reconstructed markets, small capacity changes restore existence whenever no stable matching exists at the original capacities.
tldr: This paper studies capacity modification in the Hospitals/Residents problem with couples, developing integer programming formulations to restore stable matchings via minimal capacity changes.
motivation: Stable matching markets with couples often fail to admit stable matchings, so understanding how small capacity adjustments can restore existence is practically and theoretically important.
method: The authors develop Exact and Cutoff integer programming formulations for jointly determining hospital capacities and a stable matching under strict couple preferences, with both members of a couple matched together or not at all.
result: Changing each hospital capacity by at most two (total increase at most one, tight bound) guarantees a stable matching for arbitrary strict preferences; sub-responsive/sub-complete couple preferences require adding at most one position per hospital, totaling at most the number of couples.
conclusion: Computational experiments across 96,000 markets show Cutoff formulations excel in minimum-repair settings and scale to 30,000 doctors, with small capacity changes reliably restoring existence.

title: EVSEFuzz : A Tool For Automated Testing Of Protocol Implementations
authors: Soham Gumaste, Michael Khan, Roland Varriale, Rigel Gjomemo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32902v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rapid adoption and development of electric vehicle (EV) networks has required the expansive deployment of EV charging infrastructure (EVCI) which relies on communication protocols such as the open charge point protocol (OCPP) to coordinate data transfer between charging network operators and the EV supply equipment. In this paper, we present EVSEFuzz, a tool for automatically building fuzzers to test the security of protocol implementations. To achieve this we make a novel use of Python datatype validation packages and tools to ``understand'' datatypes and message structures and generate both compliant and non-compliant messages. To date, EVSEFuzz has been tested successfully with several open and closed-source implementations and has found several vulnerabilities leading to the publication of two CVEs.
tldr: EVSEFuzz is a tool that automatically generates fuzzers for security testing of EV charging protocol implementations such as OCPP.
motivation: The rapid growth of electric vehicle charging infrastructure creates a large attack surface in communication protocols like OCPP, motivating automated security testing of vendor implementations.
method: The tool leverages Python datatype validation packages to infer message structures and datatypes, then generates both compliant and non-compliant messages to fuzz protocol implementations.
result: EVSEFuzz was tested against several open- and closed-source implementations and uncovered multiple vulnerabilities, leading to two published CVEs.
conclusion: Automated datatype-driven fuzzing is an effective approach for hardening EV charging protocol implementations, though the work is purely in classical cybersecurity.

title: Economic Corridor Detection From Multi-Source Earth Observation And Commercial Geospatial Data Across Nigeria's Kilometre-Scale Grid
authors: Richard Oduntan
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31675v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identifying economic corridors at national scale is challenging where firm registries, transaction flows, and local economic-output statistics are incomplete or unavailable. This paper develops a reproducible multi-proxy screening framework for detecting economic-corridor candidates across Nigeria using a kilometre-scale analytical grid. The framework combines built-up land cover from ESA WorldCover, night-time light radiance from NASA VIIRS Black Marble, building-footprint density from Google Open Buildings, a static urban-intensity proxy derived from population, built-up share and night-time light level, and commercial point-of-interest density from Overture Places and OpenStreetMap. A dual proxy gate requiring both built-up evidence, defined as built-up fraction above 0.1, and night-time luminosity, defined as radiance above 1 nW cm-2 sr-1, identifies active corridor cells, which are then clustered into corridor objects and assigned interpretable typologies. The analytical frame contains 762,751 cells: national, state, and geopolitical-zone summaries use 749,191 canonical national-grid cells, while 13,560 configured metropolitan area-of-interest overlay cells are reserved for an eight-metro comparison. Applied to Nigeria, the framework identifies 11,243 active corridor cells on the national grid, representing 1.50% of cells, and 598 corridor objects spanning 10,682 retained cells and approximately 36.3 million people. Corridor activity concentrates around Lagos and other southern commercial geographies, while the method also surfaces emerging and constrained corridor candidates for review. All outputs are proxy-based screening signals for spatial planning, infrastructure prioritisation, and market-intelligence triage; they do not measure GDP, firm revenue, transaction volume, freight movement, infrastructure capacity, service adequacy, or official corridor designation.
tldr: The paper builds a reproducible multi-proxy geospatial screening framework to detect economic-corridor candidates across Nigeria on a kilometre-scale grid.
motivation: National-scale economic corridor identification is difficult where firm registries, transaction flows, and local economic-output statistics are missing or incomplete.
method: It combines ESA WorldCover built-up land cover, NASA VIIRS night-time lights, Google Open Buildings footprint density, an urban-intensity proxy, and commercial POI density from Overture Places and OpenStreetMap, applying a dual gate (built-up fraction > 0.1 and radiance > 1 nW cm-2 sr-1) before clustering corridor cells into objects with typologies.
result: Across 762,751 grid cells, the framework flags 11,243 active corridor cells (1.50%) grouped into 598 corridor objects covering about 36.3 million people, concentrated around Lagos and southern commercial zones, with emerging and constrained candidates also surfaced.
conclusion: The outputs are proxy-based screening signals for spatial planning, infrastructure prioritisation, and market-intelligence triage, not measures of GDP, revenue, freight, or official corridor designation.

title: Intermittency In Firm Bankruptcies From Register Data
authors: D. Diemer F. P. Pijpers
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32376v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: By analysing the clustering of bankruptcy activity from administrative register data in the Netherlands over time, the intermittency of this process is investigated. Using methodology from survival analysis a statistical characterization of bursts is obtained: short active periods alternating with quieter periods. Using Statistics Netherlands microdata on Dutch business bankruptcies declared on court hearing-days from 2009 to 2024, combined with input-output tables from the Dutch national accounts, it is studied whether this clustering can be explained by differences between sectors, years, and inter-sectoral exposure. Sector differences explain most of the heterogeneity in the data, while year effects matter to a lesser extent and the inter-sectoral exposure variables constructed from the input-output tables further improve model fit.
tldr: The paper studies intermittency and clustering in Dutch business bankruptcies using administrative register microdata and survival-analysis methods.
motivation: The authors aim to characterize bursts of bankruptcy activity over time and test whether clustering can be explained by sector, year, and inter-sectoral exposure.
method: They analyze court-declared bankruptcies from 2009 to 2024 using survival-analysis techniques and combine Statistics Netherlands microdata with input-output tables to model sectoral and exposure effects.
result: Sector differences explain most heterogeneity, year effects matter less, and inter-sectoral exposure variables improve model fit.
conclusion: Bankruptcy activity exhibits intermittent clustering that is largely sector-driven, with additional explanatory power from inter-sectoral linkages.

title: Finite Element Approximation On Piecewise Smooth Domains
authors: Lucia Gastaldi Daniele Boffi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31822v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The approximation theory by finite elements is usually described on the simplified geometry of polygonal or polyhedral domains. While avoiding the question of boundary approximation makes the analysis simpler, real applications may involve piecewise smooth domains and in some cases the extension of classical results to general boundaries may be tricky. In this paper we discuss in a systematic way the approximation properties and the error analysis of standard non-isoparametric finite element spaces on piecewise curvilinear domains in two and three dimensions. We show in detail how the geometric error introduces a barrier for the [MATH] and [MATH] error of the solution of both Dirichlet and Neumann elliptic problems independently of the regularity of the problem and of the degree of the finite element spaces used.
tldr: A numerical analysis paper systematically studying approximation properties and error estimates of non-isoparametric finite element spaces on piecewise curvilinear domains in 2D and 3D.
motivation: Classical finite element approximation theory is developed for polygonal/polyhedral domains, but real applications involve piecewise smooth boundaries where extending classical results is technically delicate.
method: Systematic a priori error analysis of standard non-isoparametric finite element spaces on piecewise curvilinear domains, treating Dirichlet and Neumann elliptic problems and isolating the geometric (boundary approximation) error contribution.
result: The geometric error induces a barrier on the H1 and L2 errors of the discrete solution that is independent of the regularity of the continuous problem and of the polynomial degree of the finite element space.
conclusion: Isoparametric or geometry-adapted discretizations are required to recover optimal convergence rates on curvilinear domains; non-isoparametric elements saturate at a geometry-limited accuracy.

title: Closed-form Optimal Propulsive-Differential Drag Control For Large Reconfigurations Of Spacecraft Swarms
authors: Simone D'amico Matthew Hunter
abstract: ArXiv:2610.31973v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Distributed Space Systems offer unique capabilities but have significant hardware limitations on computational processing and fuel when employing small satellites. These constraints drive interest in deterministic maneuver planning that incorporates orbital perturbations to improve final state accuracy and decrease reconfiguration delta-v cost. This paper proposes a novel closed-form, provably optimal framework to generate complete roto-translational solutions for propulsive-differential drag control of multiple satellites. The approach leverages relative orbit elements and reachable set theory to characterize all control with a single methodology that can be readily generalized to generic impulsive-continuous control. The algorithm is robust to large reconfigurations and extended control windows where differential drag is most effective.
tldr: The paper derives a closed-form, provably optimal control framework combining propulsive maneuvers with differential drag for large roto-translational reconfigurations of small-satellite swarms.
motivation: Small satellites in distributed space systems face tight limits on onboard computation and propellant, motivating deterministic maneuver planning that exploits orbital perturbations such as differential drag to cut reconfiguration delta-v.
method: The authors use relative orbit elements and reachable set theory to characterize all admissible controls within a single unified methodology, generalizing to generic impulsive-continuous control schemes.
result: The resulting algorithm yields complete roto-translational solutions that remain robust for large reconfigurations and extended control windows where differential drag is most effective.
conclusion: A closed-form optimal propulsive-differential drag controller is established as a computationally light, fuel-efficient planning tool for spacecraft swarm reconfiguration.

title: Strengthening Ac Optimal Power Flow Relaxation Through Offline Bound Tightening And Linear Approximations
authors: Xiangxin An, Constance Crozier, Santanu S. Dey
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32006v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The alternating-current optimal power flow (ACOPF) problem is fundamental to power system operation and planning, but its nonconvexity makes globally optimal solutions of large-scale instances computationally challenging. Convex relaxations provide tractable lower bounds for assessing solution quality and supporting global optimization, although their effectiveness depends strongly on relaxation strength. This paper proposes an offline convexification and bound tightening framework for constructing strong linear programming (LP) relaxations for families of related ACOPF instances. Rather than repeating the tightening procedure for each instance, we compute variable bounds and second-order cone outer-approximation (SOC-OA) cuts offline using a demand-slack model and reuse them for subsequent instances with the same topology and admissible demand variations. Computational results on PGLib instances show that the fully offline approach achieves an average gap of [MATH], compared with [MATH] for the fully online approach, while achieving an average speedup of approximately [MATH]. The results demonstrate that offline convexification and bound tightening can recover most of the relaxation improvement of online tightening while significantly reducing the computational burden for repeated ACOPF evaluations.
tldr: This paper proposes an offline convexification and bound-tightening framework that reuses precomputed variable bounds and SOC outer-approximation cuts to build strong LP relaxations for families of AC optimal power flow instances with shared topology.
motivation: ACOPF is nonconvex, so globally optimal solutions for large instances are hard; convex relaxations give tractable lower bounds, but their strength depends on expensive per-instance tightening, which is wasteful when many related instances must be solved.
method: Variable bounds and second-order cone outer-approximation (SOC-OA) cuts are computed offline using a demand-slack model and then reused for subsequent instances sharing the same topology and admissible demand variations.
result: On PGLib instances the fully offline approach reaches an average gap close to the fully online approach while delivering roughly an order-of-magnitude speedup.
conclusion: Offline convexification and bound tightening recovers most of the relaxation strength of online tightening while substantially reducing computation for repeated ACOPF evaluations.

title: A Branch-and-filter Method For Mixed-integer Linear Programming
authors: Nikos Dimou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32165v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We develop a new tree-search framework for mixed-integer linear programming problems, which incorporates a filter mechanism as a node-acceptance device. The introduced branch-and-filter algorithm combines proper branching actions with a filter on integrality violation and an incumbent-dependent objective coordinate. Inspired by classical filter methods in nonconvex constrained optimization, the proposed method moves to a restoration phase whenever sufficient progress cannot be provided by the filter and funnel mechanisms, the latter of which is anchored at global relaxation lower bounds. Under mild assumptions, the introduced method either certifies infeasibility in finitely many iterations, or converges to global optimality. Moreover, we establish a total outer iteration complexity bound of order [MATH] to certification of an [MATH]-optimal mixed-integer solution through fixed-integer linear programming recovery. We finally perform several numerical experiments to study the performance of branch-and-filter against benchmark solvers, under a branch-and-bound, a branch-and-cut, and a novel cell-deletion realization of the proposed restoration oracle.
tldr: The paper introduces a branch-and-filter tree-search algorithm for mixed-integer linear programming that uses filter and funnel mechanisms as node-acceptance criteria within a branch-and-bound/cut framework.
motivation: Classical filter methods from nonconvex constrained optimization offer a principled way to handle competing criteria (integrality violation and objective value), motivating their transfer to MILP tree search.
method: The algorithm combines branching with a filter on integrality violation and an incumbent-dependent objective coordinate, invoking a restoration phase with funnel mechanisms anchored at global relaxation lower bounds when progress stalls.
result: Under mild assumptions the method either certifies infeasibility in finitely many iterations or converges to global optimality, with a total outer iteration complexity bound for reaching an epsilon-optimal integer solution via fixed-integer LP recovery; numerical experiments compare it against benchmark solvers across branch-and-bound, branch-and-cut, and a novel cell-deletion restoration oracle.
conclusion: Branch-and-filter provides a convergent, complexity-bounded alternative tree-search framework for MILP, though it lies entirely within classical mathematical optimization.

title: Global Injectivity And Real Jacobian Conjecture In $\mathbb{R}^n$
authors: Xinhao Hu, Jaume Llibre, Yilei Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32391v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we study the global injectivity of local diffeomorphisms in [MATH], extending the criterions of Braun and Llibre in [{\it Pacific J. Math.} {\bf 333} (2024) 1--15] from the planar radial case to arbitrary dimension. Then we extend the results of Llibre and Mello in [{\it Bull. Sci. Math.} {\bf 213} (2026) 103889] to arbitrary dimension, obtaining two necessary and sufficient conditions for the real Jacobian conjecture in [MATH] by qualitative theory of differential equations. Finally, using weighted Poincar\'e compactification in [MATH], we provide a sufficient condition for the real Jacobian conjecture.
tldr: The paper studies global injectivity of local diffeomorphisms in R^n and provides conditions for the real Jacobian conjecture using qualitative ODE theory and weighted Poincaré compactification.
motivation: The real Jacobian conjecture and global injectivity of local diffeomorphisms are central problems in real algebraic geometry and dynamical systems, with prior results mainly limited to planar or radial settings.
method: The authors extend Braun–Llibre and Llibre–Mello criteria from planar radial cases to arbitrary dimension, using qualitative theory of differential equations and weighted Poincaré compactification.
result: They obtain two necessary and sufficient conditions for the real Jacobian conjecture in R^n and a sufficient condition via weighted Poincaré compactification.
conclusion: The work advances pure mathematical understanding of global injectivity and the real Jacobian conjecture, but has no direct connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: SynMark: Semantic-Coordinate Multi-Bit Watermarking During Llm Code Generation
authors: Rui Xu, Weizhi Liu, Zhaoxia Yin
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32017v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: LLM-generated code is increasingly reused across downstream applications and often undergoes identifier renaming or structural refactoring, making robustness to functionality-preserving edits essential for generative multi-bit code watermarking. Existing methods commonly derive message routes from surface-token prefixes, so such edits can desynchronize routing and degrade watermark recovery. We propose SynMark, which replaces surface-dependent routing with learned semantic coordinates and further calibrates residual recovery errors after transformation. For watermark embedding, Scope learns semantic coordinates from aligned prefixes of functionally equivalent variants for keyed routing and applies a syntax-aware adaptive bias during generation. For watermark extraction, Traced recomputes semantic routes from transformed code and uses reliability-weighted aggregation to suppress unreliable token contributions. Under 100% identifier renaming, SynMark retains 82.27% and 83.77% BitAcc on CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder, respectively. Across three code LMs, it also improves clean BitAcc and Pass@1 by up to 4.53 and 11.18 percentage points over the strongest watermarked baselines.
tldr: SynMark is a multi-bit watermarking scheme for LLM-generated code that uses learned semantic coordinates instead of surface-token prefixes to keep message routing robust under identifier renaming and refactoring.
motivation: Existing multi-bit code watermarks route message bits via surface-token prefixes, so functionality-preserving edits such as renaming desynchronize the routing and break watermark recovery.
method: The embedding component (Scope) learns semantic coordinates from aligned prefixes of functionally equivalent code variants for keyed routing and injects a syntax-aware adaptive bias during generation, while the extraction component (Traced) recomputes semantic routes from transformed code and aggregates token contributions with reliability weighting.
result: Under 100% identifier renaming SynMark retains 82.27% and 83.77% BitAcc on CodeLlama and DeepSeek-Coder, and across three code LMs it improves clean BitAcc and Pass@1 by up to 4.53 and 11.18 percentage points over the strongest watermarked baselines.
conclusion: Semantic-coordinate routing plus residual-error calibration yields code watermarks that survive semantics-preserving transformations without sacrificing code quality, though the work lies outside quantum information science.

title: Automated Post-Exploitation Attack Chain Exploration Based On A Phase-guided Hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search Algorithm
authors: Jie Ying, Mengce Zheng, Ruoxi Chen, Wenrui Cheng, Tiantian Zhu, Zhongjie Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.32278v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Advanced attackers in post-exploitation scenarios increasingly craft attack chains that combine benign operations, configuration errors, and vulnerability exploitation to achieve objectives like privilege escalation. While such chains pose significant threats, manually discovering them in complex modern host environments is prohibitively labor-intensive. Automating this discovery is therefore essential for proactive defense, yet existing methods still suffer from inefficiency and lack diversity when exploring these attack chains. To address these limitations, we present APEX, an Automated Post-EXploitation attack chain exploration system. This system transforms attack chain discovery into a planning problem and solves it with a novel phase-guided hybrid Planning-Monte Carlo Tree Search (MCTS) algorithm. By organizing attack actions into semantic phases and integrating symbolic planning with MCTS, APEX enables efficient exploration of the state space while generating multiple diverse chains. Evaluations on a benchmark comprising 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems and 291 cloud instances demonstrate that APEX successfully discovers both known and previously unreported attack chains--including 9 novel privilege escalation vectors--providing actionable intelligence for hardening complex production environments.
tldr: APEX automates post-exploitation attack-chain discovery by combining semantic phase guidance with hybrid symbolic planning and Monte Carlo Tree Search.
motivation: Manual discovery of complex post-exploitation attack chains is labor-intensive, while existing automated methods are inefficient and produce limited diversity.
method: The paper formulates attack-chain discovery as a planning problem and solves it using a phase-guided hybrid Planning-MCTS algorithm that organizes actions into semantic phases and integrates symbolic planning with MCTS.
result: Evaluated on 5 virtual machines, 30 synthetic problems, and 291 cloud instances, APEX found known and previously unreported attack chains, including 9 novel privilege-escalation vectors.
conclusion: APEX provides actionable intelligence for hardening production environments by efficiently exploring diverse post-exploitation attack chains.
